editorials.title: Water wealth: On groundwater exploitation in Punjab
editorials.passage:
That Punjab is over-extracting groundwater is not news. According to the 2025-26 Dynamic Groundwater Assessment , its groundwater extraction rate was 152% . While interventions reduced the number of ‘over-exploited’ blocks by five over the last two assessments, 72% of its 153 blocks are in the ‘red zone’, the highest among States. The principal consumer is irrigation for rice and wheat, amounting to nearly 25 billion cubic metres a year in the latest estimate. Data also show that the fraction of observation wells with water below 40 metres in the post-monsoon period grew by two percentage points between 2022 and 2025. What began as a strategy to improve food security eventually yielded a concentrated rice-wheat cropping system, in which assured procurement, subsidised electricity and access to groundwater made high-yield varieties, intensive irrigation and fertilizer use and mechanisation less risky than alternative modes of cultivation. In the same vein, the reluctance of the region’s farmers to pursue other crops due to uncertainties in storage options, prices, processing infrastructure, and supply chains has gone relatively unaddressed. But as the water crisis persists, the wealth gap among farmers is also widening. A recent study in the Economic and Political Weekly noted that while farmers with marginal landholdings use water more efficiently, wealthier farmers are better equipped to access lower water tables as well as draw higher volumes. So, as the water table drops, those unable to afford the requisite tube wells are forced to buy water, transferring their wealth to larger landowners and creating unregulated dependencies. A different study by two members of the same team, published in Discover Sustainability, reported that in Sangrur and Barnala, larger farms earned higher returns but recorded lower groundwater productivity vis-à-vis paddy, than smaller farms. Effectively, groundwater depletion raises the capital required for irrigation, which systematically privileges those farmers with better access to finance.

State governments continue to attempt to address the demand pressure in multiple ways even as the scale continues to overwhelm the resulting gains in efficiency. At this juncture, together with those efforts, the State should also endeavour to protect farmers’ incomes and access to irrigation while rendering the cost of additional extraction prohibitive. The ‘Pani Bachao, Paisa Kamao’ scheme, in which farmers are entitled to cash for every unused kilowatt-hour (for pumping) under a threshold, is already promising, albeit with low enrolment. Broadly, the State should use part of the electricity subsidy bill to directly support smallholder farmers, help collectivise irrigation infrastructure, and/or support farmers’ transition to other crops. When benefits follow the cultivator, including tenants, rather than owners of the land or pumps, welfare can subsidise access to water rather than groundwater extraction.

editorials.title: Freezing democracy: On the Election Commission of India and West Bengal
editorials.passage:
Almost 28 years after Mamata Banerjee set up the All India Trinamool Congress and designed its symbol of ‘grass and flowers’, the Election Commission of India (ECI) on September 17, 2026, froze the party’s name and symbol . The 14-page order stated that since two rival groups — one led by Ms. Banerjee and the other by Arup Roy — are now claiming to be the party, the matter requires “substantive determination”, and neither group can use the party’s name or symbol. The ECI has allotted new names and symbols to both groups. The ECI’s move has effectively denied Ms. Banerjee of her party’s name and symbol. For nearly three decades, crores of voters have placed their faith in the party’s name and symbol, elected Ms. Banerjee as Chief Minister of West Bengal three times, and sent scores as its MPs to Parliament. Even in the April 2026 West Bengal Assembly polls , 41% of the electorate, or more than 2.60 crore voters, voted for Ms. Banerjee’s party , while the margin between it and the Bharatiya Janata Party was only about 32 lakh votes. Opposition parties, including the Congress, have said that similar attempts to freeze the name and symbol were made in the case of the Shiv Sena, calling such action of freezing the name and the symbol as “party theft” and a case of democratic decline.

Political parties are organic entities that keep democracy vibrant and alive and any attempts to engineer their dissolution is an attack on the very foundations of India’s democracy. If a political party has to wither away, it should happen only through the determination of the people. Serious questions have been raised about the role of the ECI, which held the West Bengal Assembly polls in 2026 after a hurriedly organised Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of the electoral rolls that left lakhs of voters out, and is now freezing the name and symbol of the principal Opposition party. Free and fair elections form the bedrock of the republic. When political parties, which are engines for ensuring that the will of the electorate is reflected through free and fair elections, are dismantled and stripped of their names and symbols, the ECI cannot absolve itself of responsibility or hide behind processes and practices. The BJP leadership in West Bengal has repeatedly claimed that, after the Assembly polls, there would be no existence of the Trinamool Congress as a party. The ECI’s acts of omission and commission clearly suggest that it is acting in tandem with the interests of the BJP.

editorials.title: IIT must ensure probe into tragedy, follow with reforms
editorials.passage: Developments at IIT Bombay following the death of reserved-category student Sahil Wakode deserve a calmer reading than the noise around the campus has allowed. The institute has reversed its earlier statement, acknowledging that it was inappropriate to present matters as settled before an inquiry. The students have issued a more measured statement, clarifying that their protest was not to defend cheating, but that the death raises questions beyond the exam violation. That distinction is important.Wakode’s parents’ anguish cannot be set aside. They have repeatedly alleged caste-based harassment. The institute has maintained it had not received a complaint earlier. The police have registered a case under the SC and ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, and the professor named has been removed from his administrative position pending inquiry. These matters require a fair and independent investigation, not competing claims. If Wakode violated exam rules, consequences were called for. But discipline must be administered fairly, transparently and without humiliation. An allegation of discrimination, meanwhile, cannot be dismissed based on the exam violation. Both questions require evidence..The students’ latest statement offers an opening. Their demands have been placed before the institute’s director, who has acknowledged them even as calls for his resignation continue. An open house also allowed students to put their concerns directly to the administration. The task now is to turn this into real change: credible grievance mechanisms, transparent disciplinary procedures, support for students under pressure and an impartial probe of discrimination allegations.IITs reflect a contradiction visible elsewhere in India. The country is expanding its technological and scientific capacity even as hierarchy, patriarchy, authority and exclusion continue to shape everyday life in classrooms, offices, hospitals and public institutions. Political polarisation tends to deepen these divisions. The lessons and victories of the Jantar Mantar protest must not be ignored or frittered away by the stakeholders concerned. Matters must now move from accusation to inquiry and reform.For Wakode’s parents, nothing can undo their loss. The least the institution can offer is honesty and a process they can trust. Students, too, have a responsibility to keep raising difficult questions without politicising the search for accountability. The institution shoulders the greater responsibility: students from different backgrounds should encounter the same rules and receive the same dignity. editorials.title: Keralam must not return to powerless days of the 1980s
editorials.passage: The ongoing power crisis in Keralam draws striking parallels to the 1980s, a time when unexpected load-shedding and wild voltage fluctuations were part of daily life. It is not much different now. With rainfall scarce and demand surging, the state is grappling with a severe power shortage and unannounced outages. One might jest that the situation aligns with the recent social media trend of turning the clock back to the 1980s, but the people’s pain is real and the joke is on the Kerala State Electricity Board and successive governments that have done precious little to enhance capacity to cope with growing demand. Over the last three decades, Keralam has not seen any significant addition to its generation capacity, with the last big project commissioned in 1997. Some smaller projects have come up, but not enough to meet the rising demand. To power itself, Keralam has made a habit of plugging into other states’ capacities and the national grid.The state’s daily peak power demand—which crossed 6,000 megawatts earlier this year—averages at about 4,800 MW. The availability, on the other hand, is only around 4,200 MW. The gap forces the state to ‘beg, borrow or steal’. While it looks to beg and borrow from other states on a daily basis, the power utility also has indulged in unauthorised overdrawing from the national grid, risking penalties. The irony is that Keralam has an installed solar capacity of nearly 2,500 MW, but the supply is erratic. Demand peaks in the night and the state lacks the infrastructure to store solar power..The sight needs to be fixed on long-term solutions beyond the ongoing political blame-game. Growth in power consumption is a natural fallout of urbanisation and economic advancement. Hence, the solution lies in raising supply rather than regulating demand. Since new projects are likely to face environmental and societal hurdles, Keralam must speed up plans for pumped storage generation at the existing hydel plants. It can also go for large-scale battery storage systems to make efficient use of its renewable capacity.Back in the 1980s, people put up with outages because they did not know any better. But a modern society demands uninterrupted supply. Going back to 1980s is not an option for the people, neither is it for the government..Follow The New Indian Express channel on WhatsApp Download the TNIE app to stay with us and follow the latest

editorials.title: Quick Take | Sustainable festivals
editorials.passage: Like at every festive season, water bodies across India are handing their cities humongous bills for ecological damages. The Greater Chennai Corporation has cleared as much as 139 tonnes of waste from five beaches following Vinayagar or Ganesh Chaturthi immersions over the weekend. Last year, the Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation dredged up 1,982 tonnes of plaster of Paris following the same festival. This year, although the municipality has built 383 artificial ponds to curb pollutants leaking into public water bodies, it has simultaneously planned for worse outcomes. The National Green Tribunal’s 2015 bar on immersing non-biodegradable and other toxic materials is still observed mostly in breach. If we do not make our festivals pollution-free today, we will cede the right to demand cleaner water, air and soil tomorrow..Follow The New Indian Express channel on WhatsApp Download the TNIE app to stay with us and follow the latest

editorials.title: Hindi as a bridge
editorials.passage:
September is observed as Hindi Month in India. Hindi Day was celebrated across the country on September 14, and Hindi Fortnight is being observed from September 15 to 30. Hindi month is more than an occasion to celebrate a language. It is an opportunity to reflect on Hindi’s remarkable journey, its expanding global presence, and, equally importantly, the contribution of those who did not speak Hindi as their mother tongue but devoted their lives to nurturing and enriching it. 

On 14 September 1949, the Constituent Assembly adopted Hindi in the Devanagari script as the official language of the Union. Since then, September 14 has been observed as Hindi Diwas. Over the decades, however, Hindi has moved far beyond the boundaries of an official-language debate. It has emerged as a major language of literature, journalism, education, cinema, popular culture and digital communication. It is among the world’s most widely spoken languages and is spoken or understood by communities in more than a hundred countries. The global journey of Hindi also tells a story of linguistic openness. Its development has never been the exclusive achievement of native Hindi speakers. 

Scholars, writers, journalists, teachers and intellectuals from Bengal, Maharashtra, the South, the Northeast and even distant countries have made substantial contributions to its growth. Their work reminds us that a language becomes truly universal not by excluding other languages but by creating bridges among them. Interestingly, some of the foundational chapters of modern Hindi were written outside the Hindi-speaking region. The development of Hindi prose received an important impetus at Fort William College in Calcutta. Lallu Lal composed Prem Sagar there in 1810, a work widely regarded as an important milestone in the history of Hindi prose. Calcutta also witnessed another landmark in Hindi’s history when Udant Martand, the first Hindi newspaper, began publication on 30 May 1826. 

More than a century later, the University of Calcutta awarded its first M.A. degree in Hindi in 1921 to Nalini Mohan Sanyal. These facts are not merely historical curiosities. They challenge the narrow assumption that Hindi belongs only to the geographical regions where it is traditionally spoken. Its history demonstrates that people from different linguistic backgrounds have repeatedly adopted Hindi as a medium of intellectual and cultural exchange. Bengal, in particular, made an extraordinary contribution to the development of Hindi. 

Figures such as Tarini Charan Mitra, Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar, Keshav Chandra Sen, Raja Ram Mohan Roy, Shyam Sundar Sen, Chintamani Ghosh, Sharda Charan Mitra, Amrit Lal Chakravarty, Rajnarayan Basu, Ramananda Chattopadhyay, Sri Aurobindo, Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay, Rabindranath Tagore and Nalini Mohan Sanyal were associated in various ways with the intellectual and cultural world in which Hindi developed and expanded. The nationalist movement further strengthened this linguistic interaction. Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose delivered a historic speech supporting Hindi in Calcutta on 20 December 1928, as chairman of the reception committee of the Rashtrabhasha Conference. 

His advocacy reflected the larger nationalist aspiration for a language capable of connecting people across India’s linguistic diversity. Maharashtra too produced remarkable contributors to Hindi. Baburao Vishnu Paradkar, one of the towering figures of Hindi journalism, came from a Marathispeaking background. His contribution to Hindi journalism demonstrates how linguistic identity and linguistic service can coexist harmoniously. Madhavrao Sapre, Lakshman Narayan Garde, Prabhakar Machwe, Muktibodh, Damodar Khadse, Manohar Khadilkar, Rajendra Dhopadkar, Ajit Wadnerkar and many others represent a long tradition of Marathi-speaking scholars and writers who enriched Hindi journalism, literature and criticism. 

The same spirit can be seen in southern India. Scholars such as M. K. Damodaran Unni, G. Gopinathan, N. Chandrasekharan Nair, Vishwanatha Iyer, Subramania Bharati, B.V. Karanth, Moturi Satyanarayana, Bala Shauri Reddy and Yarlagadda Lakshmi Prasad, among others, contributed to the teaching, propagation, translation and intellectual development of Hindi. Their work helped Hindi cross regional boundaries and enter new educational and cultural spaces. The Northeast has also contributed to this wider Hindi landscape. Gopinath Bordoloi, Bineshwar Brahma, Piyong Temjan Jamir, Paresh Chandra Devsharma, Rajanikant Chakravarti, Navinchandra Kalita and the Manipuri scholar Acharya Radhagovind Thongam are among those associated with the promotion of Hindi in a region celebrated for its extraordinary linguistic diversity. 

Hindi’s global expansion becomes even more striking when we look beyond India. Foreign scholars have played an exceptional role in studying, teaching, translating and documenting Hindi and Hindustani. The French scholar Garcin de Tassy devoted his life to the study of Hindustani and produced the first major history of Hindi literature, Histoire de la littérature hindouie et hindoustanie. At a time when Hindi and Urdu were often discussed under the broader category of Hindustani, his scholarship helped introduce Indian languages and literature to European intellectual circles. George Grierson, an English linguist, undertook the monumental Linguistic Survey of India, documenting hundreds of languages and dialects. 

His scholarship demonstrated the extraordinary linguistic richness of India and drew attention to literary traditions associated with figures such as Vidyapati and Tulsidas. The Belgian scholar Father Camille Bulcke represents perhaps one of the most moving examples of a foreigner's intellectual and cultural commitment to India. He earned his M.A. in Hindi literature from Allahabad University in 1947 and completed his doctoral research on Ramkatha: Origin and Development in 1949. His English-Hindi Dictionary, published in 1968, became an important reference work. His profound engagement with the Ramkatha tradition and Tulsidas made him an enduring figure in Hindi studies. Russian scholar Yevgeny Petrovich Chelyshev made significant contributions to the study of modern Hindi poetry. Chinese scholar Zhong Tinghan translated major Hindi works, including Tulsidas’s Ramcharitmanas, Premchand's Nirmala and Yashpal’s Jhootha Sach, into Chinese. 

German scholar Lothar Lutze translated Hindi, Bengali and Kannada literature into German and wrote extensively on Hindi literature. Japanese scholar Prof. Kyuya translated Premchand's Godaan into Japanese and contributed important dictionaries and textbooks. Among Western scholars, Cambridge professor Ronald Stuart McGregor occupies a distinguished place. His work as a grammarian, translator and scholar of Hindi literature helped establish Hindi studies in academic institutions outside India. His Outline of Hindi Grammar became an important textbook for students of Hindi in Europe and elsewhere. The lesson from this history is clear: the making of Hindi has been a collective enterprise. Its growth has been nourished by people belonging to different regions, linguistic traditions and cultures. 

Hindi’s strength lies precisely in this capacity to absorb, communicate and connect. Yet the task before Hindi today is different. The digital age has transformed the way languages compete and coexist. Hindi must expand its presence in higher education, scientific research, technology, artificial intelligence, digital publishing and global academic discourse. Translation into and from Hindi must become a much larger enterprise. The language must be equipped to express contemporary knowledge without losing its literary richness and cultural depth. Hindi Diwas, therefore, should not be reduced to ceremonial speeches and official programmes. 

It should become an occasion for honest introspection. If Hindi is to become a genuinely global language, it must welcome the contributions of other Indian languages and cultures rather than viewing linguistic diversity as a threat. The history of Hindi itself offers the answer. From Calcutta to Cambridge, from Maharashtra to the Northeast, and from France and Belgium to Russia, China, Germany and Japan, countless scholars have helped Hindi travel beyond its traditional boundaries. 

Hundreds of scholars in more than a hundred countries continue to teach, research, translate and promote Hindi. Their work demonstrates that Hindi’s future is not confined to one region. It belongs to everyone who believes that language is a bridge between cultures. The most appropriate way to celebrate Hindi Diwas, therefore, is to recognize this inclusive legacy and build upon it. Hindi can become a truly global language only when it speaks not merely for one linguistic community but with the many languages and cultures of India and the world. Its future will depend not on linguistic isolation, but on its ability to communicate India’s diverse intellectual and cultural heritage to humanity.  

(The writer is a Professor at Mahatma Gandhi Anterrashtriya Hindi Vishwavidyalaya (a Central University), Wardha, Maharashtra)

editorials.title: Resilient policies to mitigate heat waves
editorials.passage:
What if the deadliest natural disaster of the 21st century is not a flood, earthquake, cyclone, or drought, but the silent, unremitting increase in temperature? Heat waves are no longer a seasonal inconvenience; they are a major public policy challenge. They threaten economic productivity, particularly for informal workers; increase health risks, including respiratory and cardiovascular diseases; reduce staple crop yields; disrupt food supply chains; and hinder sustainable development. 

According to the IMD report for June 2026, Sriganganagar in Rajasthan experienced the highest maximum temperature of 45.1°, but the same place recorded 48° during 2025. The year 2025 is recorded as the eighth warmest year, with a rise of 0.28° from the 1991-2020 average temperature; however, 2026 is considered the hottest year, with widespread and prolonged heatwaves with massive consequences. In April 2026, on a single day, India set an unwanted record, where all fifty of the world’s hottest cities were in the country. By May, this figure had increased to 97 out of the top 100, with Balangiri in Odisha recording a breach of 48 degrees Celsius. 

The Urban Heat effect has been significant in metropolitan cities due to dense construction, industrial waste, and glass-fronted buildings, causing a rise in temperature of 2° to 3°. Reports indicate a similar rise in northern, central, and western states, with severe alerts in Delhi-NCR, Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, and Rajasthan. According to the WHO, temperature, frequency and intensity of heat waves will rise in the 21st century as a result of climate change. High air temperatures can affect human health and cause additional deaths. 

The impact of heat waves on health can extend beyond direct heat-related illnesses like heat stroke, dehydration, respiratory and cardiovascular issues, and hyperthermia, abnormal high body temperature caused by the body’s inability to regulate heat. Heat waves also trigger indirect health risks by increasing the probability of snake bites, vector-borne diseases and human-wildlife conflicts as extreme heat alters animal behaviour, which drives animals from wildlife into places where humans live in search of water, food and cold enclosures. Reports indicate that within a two-month span during the summer months, Kerala witnessed over 60 snake bite cases with eight snakebite deaths from six districts, making it the deadliest season so far and with six people losing their lives within a single week. 

Studies show that a single day of extreme heat causes about 3,400 excess deaths across India, while a five-day heatwave causes nearly 30,000 deaths. According to IMD data between 2000 and 2020, over 10,000 people lost their lives due to extreme heatwaves in India. Census officials, government teachers, gig workers, and other informal workers who are exposed to outside work and become heat victims go unrecorded or unreported. These lives and deaths remain dry statistics, and as heat waves become more frequent and severe in India, protecting public health will require a transformation from emergency response to advance planning and long-term climate risk management. 

Beyond their health impacts, heatwaves also have substantial economic consequences, reducing labour productivity through their effects on mental health, economic well-being, and behavioural patterns. As per reports of the ILO’s Working on a Warmer Planet, India lost 4.3 per cent of working hours due to heat stress in 1995; this is projected to increase by 5.8 per cent by 2030. Additionally, McKinsey supports the study by revealing that chronic exposure to heat decreases productivity and efficiency, with loss of labour hours putting 2.5 to 4.5 per cent of GDP at risk by 2030. Mumbai street vendors face 30-40 per cent income drops from spoiled goods and severe health issues due to extreme heat, exacerbated by a lack of protective policy. 

Foreseeing these situations, Kerala introduced midday breaks from noon to 3 p.m. However, there has been a lack of compliance, specifically in the informal sector among gig workers, construction workers, and other outdoor workers. According to the NITI Aayog report published in 2022, India’s gig workforce is expected to increase to 23 million, making it extremely necessary to take measures to tackle this rise in temperatures. Instead of focusing on maximising profits with higher working hours, employers and policymakers should prioritise workers' health and well-being. The National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA) has issued guidelines to manage heatwave risks, but their enforcement has been limited. Therefore, stronger monitoring, enforcement, and accountability from the government are required to protect vulnerable workers from extreme heat exposure. 

Evidence also suggests that heatwaves reduce agricultural productivity by straining water and land resources, damaging crops, and depleting the farm output ratio. This raises concerns about food security in the country. Extreme heat waves have caused various environmental degradations in India this year. Heatwaves have triggered issues like droughts and wildfires across central and peninsular areas, causing damage to forests and biodiversity. High temperature causes rapid evaporation of soil moisture, affecting agricultural land and long-term soil health, which affects food security. 

A compounding public health burden was particularly evident in North Indian cities, driven by deteriorating air quality during heatwave s, compounded by dust storms from Rajasthan and wildfire smoke. The government has implemented various policy recommendations; however, they have failed to achieve their objectives. As mentioned earlier, Kerala’s example was one of the common ones. Apart from this, a major government strategy to tackle heatwaves in Ahmedabad was the Ahmedabad Heat Action Plan (HAP), South Asia’s first municipal adaptation strategy, launched in 2013 in response to the devastating 2010 heatwaves. It has been moderately successful in controlling heat-related mortality. Despite these mechanisms, the plan faces severe structural and inclusivity challenges. 

In all of these cases, plans are prepared for the state level and don't reflect or address the problems faced by particular districts or specific communities. Plans should vary from district to district and community to community, based on economic, social, cultural, and environmental factors; therefore, state plans cannot deal with vulnerabilities caused by heatwaves in a particular district or community. Every degree rise in the temperature is testing the resilience of our cities and systems. 

These circumstances demand that the government provide practical interventions with a monitored approach, specifically mist stations which could potentially reduce the temperature by 4-5°C, incorporate vertical gardening in buildings, which could reduce the trapping of heat inside the buildings, and reduce the temperature; additionally, reducing the demand for air conditioning, thereby resulting in a diminishing demand for electricity and greenhouse emissions. 

Moreover, cities should also invest in green spaces, urban forests, and green corridors. Introduction of rest areas, access to drinking water, scheduled breaks, and flexible working hours, when properly implemented and monitored, helps construction workers, farmers, delivery boys, and other outdoor workers combat heat. Collectively, these measures, when properly implemented, would reduce the Urban Heat Island effect. 

(The writers are undergraduate students and an Assistant Professor, Department of Economics, CHRIST (deemed to be university), Bengaluru)

editorials.title: Lines that worry us and lines that don’t
editorials.passage:
Since I started doing research in 2012, I have on multiple occasions come across academic works using maps of India that are not constitutionally validated. Dissertations, research papers, presentations, and course materials frequently include them, with the authors seemingly importing them from unchecked online sources. Departments, review committees, and publications often approve these maps even though they wrongly show India’s boundaries. Throughout my years of research, this has been a consistent problem, not an isolated incident. This is the unsettling reality lying at the core of India’s concerns with a map that portrays its territorial integrity. 

The National Map Policy of 2005 has worked in that direction - for instance, the Open Series Maps developed by the Survey of India for civilian use have deliberately blurred out ‘vulnerable points’ and done away with the grid reference system, unlike the Defence Series Maps. That policy-level caution to restrict visibility of critical infrastructure is insufficient, as they are accurately identifiable through satellite images available on handheld devices. The same level of consciousness is invisible over the maps that are quietly made and circulated to challenge India’s territorial integrity. 

The element that should worry every Indian reader is that shapefiles, the fundamental data structures needed to create maps in geographic information system (GIS) software, can be easily accessed from foreign open-data sites. Indian students and researchers often download these ready-made files to use in their theses, dissertations, and working papers. But most of them fail to take cognizance of the fact that these maps have demarcated Pakistan-Occupied Jammu and Kashmir as a part of Pakistan. It gets copied, pasted, and released again instead of being fixed where it happened. It appears in master’s theses and is argued before university panels. 

It appears in works sent to journals for review by other experts. It keeps circulating without being called out for its unconstitutional portrayal. Nobody in the academic pipeline views the nation's boundary as their obligation to check, thus this self-inflicted damage continues year after year. To our dismay, these circulations beyond campuses undermine the nation’s territorial integrity and establish it as the status quo. What exists is a gap between the nation’s constitutionally mandated claim and its subversion, knowingly or unknowingly, by India’s academia. 

Recognizably, the legal system has begun to close the gap. Publishing a map that doesn’t follow the guidelines set by the Survey of India is already against the law according to the Criminal Law Amendment (Amending) Act of 1990. You can be fined or jailed for this crime. Finally, in May 2024, the University Grants Commission sent a letter to all universities, asking them to comply. The individuals making India’s maps for academic purposes had to wait for 30 years for that directive to reach their desks. 

This is where the real battle for India’s accurate maps should be fought-not in Parliament, where people complain about a tech company’s neighbourhood contest, but in every geography class, GIS lab, and thesis committee that lets an imported shapefile go through unchecked. It is not just the responsibility of the Indian Army or the Survey of India to protect the country’s borders. The onus is on Indian academia to check the maps they download from websites to save the effort required to prepare them themselves. 

Careless use jeopardises the national stand, especially in times of information warfare. The National Geospatial Policy of 2022 made the right decision by easing decades of official caution, making data available, and transforming the once-secretive Survey of India into an organization more accessible to citizens. Liberalizing the lines drawn by the citizenry accrues from the worry policy framers had. However, such a concern remains inconspicuous with lines that mediate national integrity. Each classroom and library where a map is made, shared, and never challenged either defends the territorial integrity or quietly gives it away. 

(The writer is Assistant Professor, Department of Geography, Rabindra Bharati University)

editorials.title: Nithari’s Failure
editorials.passage:
The death of Surinder Koli, years after his arrest in the Nithari killings and months after his final acquittal, leaves behind a disturbing question: what happens when a criminal justice system fails to establish the truth about crimes that have already devastated a community? The 2006 discovery of the remains of women and children near a bungalow in Nithari, on the outskirts of Delhi, exposed more than a horrific series of killings. 

It revealed the vulnerability of families whose children could disappear without their complaints receiving the urgency they deserved. Many victims belonged to poor migrant households, while the accused lived in a comparatively affluent neighbourhood. The contrast raised uncomfortable questions about whose suffering commands the attention of the state. The subsequent investigation produced multiple prosecutions and death sentences. Yet the eventual acquittals of Koli and his employer, Moninder Singh Pandher, exposed the difference between securing convictions and establishing guilt through reliable evidence. The Supreme Court's finding that Koli's confession had been extracted through torture was consequential. 

A confession obtained through coercion cannot substitute for a credible investigation, however horrifying the alleged crime. This is not an argument that acquittal proves innocence in every conceivable sense, nor does it establish who committed the killings. It is an acknowledgment that criminal responsibility must be demonstrated in court, not inferred from public outrage or the brutality of the allegations. The prosecution's failure to sustain its case leaves the victims’ families without the judicial certainty they were entitled to expect. Koli's death in Haridwar, reportedly by suicide, adds another layer of uncertainty. It must be investigated on its own evidence, without speculation about motive or circumstances. 

His death cannot retrospectively validate the prosecution’s case, just as his acquittal cannot answer every question surrounding the killings. There is also a larger institutional lesson. The Central Bureau of Investigation took over a case that had become a national scandal, but the eventual collapse of the prosecutions demonstrates why investigative credibility must be measured by the quality of evidence, not the number or severity of convictions. Allegations of torture demand scrutiny not only of investigators but also of the safeguards intended to prevent coercion and ensure accountability. The state owes these families more than expressions of sympathy. Any remaining avenues for establishing what happened should be examined through lawful, evidence-based investigation, while the circumstances of Koli’s death must be independently clarified. 

The passage of time makes that task harder, but does not diminish its importance. Nithari's enduring significance lies in this double failure: the inability to deliver reliable justice for the victims and the inability to uphold the legal protections owed to an accused person. A functioning justice system must do both. When it cannot, public outrage may produce convictions, but not truth. The final tragedy of Nithari is not simply that a man acquitted after 19 years in prison has died. It is that his death leaves the victims' families still waiting for answers that the justice system was supposed to establish.

editorials.title: Blue Again
editorials.passage:
The return of India’s hockey teams to their traditional blue jerseys at the Asian Games may look like a minor sporting correction. It is not. The controversy surrounding the brief shift to saffron has exposed a more consequential question: who gets to decide how national institutions represent the country? A jersey is not merely sportswear when it is worn by a national team. Over decades, blue has acquired an identity of its own in Indian sport. It is associated with the country’s sporting tradition and, above all, continuity. 

That does not make blue sacred, nor does it mean a different colour can never be used. But a departure from such an established symbol demands more than administrative convenience or political enthusiasm. The troubling aspect of the Hockey India episode is therefore not principally the colour saffron. It is the apparent absence of institutional process. Hockey India’s own subsequent action against its Director-General, R.K. Srivastava, has brought this issue into sharper focus. The organisation has alleged that the jersey change was implemented and publicly launched without the necessary consultation with its president or executive committee and without adequate documentary evidence of approval. That allegation, if sustained, points to a failure of governance. 

A national sporting federation cannot function as the personal domain of the office-holder who controls an administrative decision. Its authority comes from rules, procedures and collective institutional responsibility. If those safeguards can be bypassed for something as visible as a national team’s identity, there is little reason to believe that less visible decisions will receive proper scrutiny. The political dimension cannot simply be wished away either. The choice of saffron had already provoked accusations of the “saffronisation” of Indian hockey, including from former Odisha chief minister Naveen Patnaik, who alleged political involvement in the change. 

Those allegations should not be treated as established fact merely because the controversy subsequently intensified. But neither should the political sensitivity surrounding the colour have been ignored by administrators. The reversal is consequently significant. Restoring blue before the Asian Games suggests that Hockey India recognised the need to step back from a decision that had generated unnecessary controversy and institutional questions. The disciplinary action against its Director-General reinforces the impression that the manner of decision-making, not merely the outcome, has become an issue. There is a wider lesson here for Indian sport. National federations administer public-facing institutions with considerable symbolic importance. 

They should be insulated from partisan politics, but insulation also requires internal accountability. Governments, political parties, administrators and sponsors should not be allowed to convert national sporting platforms into extensions of their own preferences. India’s athletes should compete under colours chosen through transparent institutional authority, not political fashion. The return of blue is therefore welcome. More important would be ensuring that the next change ~ if there is one ~ is made for the right reasons, through the right process, and with the athletes and institution, rather than politics, at its centre

editorials.title: In deference
editorials.passage:
Within days of Xi Jinping leaving India, the Pakistan-China Boundary Joint Commission held its inaugural meeting in Islamabad. India issued a statement rejecting it in which the last paragraph demanded that Pakistan vacate territories in Kashmir under its illegal and forcible occupation. The statement was curiously silent on making a similar demand of Beijing. This is a far cry from August 2019 when the Union home minister, Amit Shah, stood in the Lok Sabha and declared that Aksai Chin is part of India and that he was ready to give his life for it. Seven years on, the same minister cannot bring himself to get in an official word about Chinese occupation.

The statement reflects the current state of India-China ties which has been evident from developments of the past few weeks: the Narendra Modi government is doing everything to ensure nothing provokes Beijing. Consider the two meetings between corps commanders that took place in the eastern sector. As we have seen from Ladakh where this mechanism was devised at China’s suggestion, such meetings take place only when there is a serious problem on the border, usually an incursion by the People’s Liberation Army into Indian territory. Video clips on social media show Chinese and Indian troops confronting each other in the Taksing area. Locals have reported Chinese encroachment and denial of movement to areas they previously accessed. Others suggest that Chinese troops have pitched tents in Indian territory and destroyed a temporary structure built by the Indian army. The government has never formally explained what was discussed, what transpired on the ground, or why no outcome was possible in the two rounds of meetings.

The silence of the Indian media is equally telling. There has been little questioning of why the corps commander talks were needed, what happened on the ground, and why there was a stalemate. Compare this to the reporting on Doklam in 2017 and eastern Ladakh in 2020 when the Modi government wanted to project that nothing had happened but source-based reporting led to extensive coverage. Now, the corporate media has evidently fallen in line with the regime’s unofficial diktat, which appears designed to meet Beijing’s demand that New Delhi rein in Indian media when it targets China. That the Modi government was trying to create a friendly and conducive environment was shockingly clear when it forced Salman Khan to rescript his film on Galwan and strip it of explicit China references. Similarly, General Anil Chauhan sought to underplay China’s active military support to Pakistan during Operation Sindoor, directly contradicting his own army deputy chief who had spoken of the deep Pakistan-China cooperation during the operation.

The aim is to project a sense of normalcy in bilateral ties, reversing the Modi government’s own dictum that the situation on the border cannot be delinked from the state of bilateral relations. Tens of thousands of troops remain deployed in harsh terrain along the Line of Actual Control, buffer zones have been created predominantly on land previously patrolled by India, and Beijing shows no inclination to discuss de-escalation. All that was put on the back burner as the narrative shifted to Xi’s visit to India for the BRICS Summit.

Much was made of the visit. Reports said Xi would arrive with a delegation of 400 and signal an economic thaw by ensuring that trade ties become more balanced. Instead, Xi stayed barely 24 hours, skipped the official dinner, and offered no concession on core Indian concerns. His bilateral meeting with Modi was an eye-opener. The two sides, going by their own official statements, talked past each other. Xi conceded nothing and did not echo even the minimal line Modi had taken.

On the border issue, Modi emphasised that peace and tranquility in the border areas remain an essential basis for the continued development of bilateral relations. Xi subsumed peace and tranquility under a parallel process of advancing bilateral ties and the boundary question simultaneously. The gap is clear: India wants the border to be the foundation on which ties are built, while China wants it to be one of the many issues to be managed while ties move forward on Beijing’s terms. Beijing has rejected clarification of the LAC since Modi raised it in 2015, maintaining that the border question should be left to future generations, echoing Deng Xiaoping’s formulation, ‘leave the problem to the next generation; they will be wiser than us.’ The special representatives’ meetings in August produced an eight-point outcome document that spoke of an Expert Group on Boundary Delimitation advancing discussions on an “[e]arly and [s]ubstantial [h]arvest” but the Group is yet to be constituted. Its first task, the document says, would be to agree on its own terms of reference. This is progress only in the most literal sense.

Instead, the Chinese readout extracted from India a commitment that its foreign policy is independent and that developing relations with China is “not subject to the influence of any third parties”, a thin euphemism for the United States of America. Modi also affirmed that India’s position on Taiwan and Tibet remains unchanged and that no force would be allowed to engage in anti-China activities on Indian territory. The Indian readout recorded no corresponding Indian counterpoint on Chinese military support to Pakistan or the Arunachal episode.

As anyone who has recently engaged with Chinese officials or scholars knows, Beijing increasingly sees India acting at the behest of Washington and seeking friendly ties with China only after being treated poorly by Trump. It indicates a breakdown of trust. More crucially, Beijing believes India has missed the bus under Modi for economic and industrial growth. It is not a peer of China and must be treated accordingly.

Beijing now operates on the assessment that India lacks the economic and political weight to demand strategic parity. A new status quo is in place, one that reflects the power asymmetry between the two nation-states. Beijing wants the normalcy that Modi seeks, but that will strictly be on China’s terms. As Xi heads to Washington for a State visit where Trump will personally receive him at the airport, Indians are left reckoning with the diminished scope of India’s strategic ambitions after 148 months of Modi in power.

Sushant Singh is lecturer at Yale University

editorials.title: Letters to the editor: Vegetarianism has extended from dinner tables to bathroom shelves
editorials.passage:
Sir — Under the current regime, vegetarianism is clearly the flavour of the season. The preoccupations have now extended from the dinner table to the bathroom shelf. A new government regulation requires the packaging of soaps, shampoos, toothpastes, and cosmetics to carry green dots to signify vegetarian ingredients and red or brown ones for non-vegetarian ingredients. If transparency is indeed the objective, perhaps the government could also focus on making information about product composition and safety more accessible. Ingredient list and regulatory safety requirements already exist but consumers may not always be given a clear picture about whether they are applying potentially harmful substances to their skin and teeth.

Sanghamitra Das, Calcutta

Sir — The president of the United States of America, Donald Trump, signed into law a Bill that allows the White House to impose 100% tariffs on major buyers of Russian oil and gas (“Rocked again”, Sept 22). As a major buyer of Russian crude, India has reason to be concerned about the economic implications, particularly amid the difficulties created by the ongoing conflict in West Asia. The fact is that savings from cheaper Russian crude are absorbed by oil company profits instead of reaching ordinary citizens.

India is not yet sufficiently developed across sectors to exercise the kind of global influence that China commands. This vulnerability has been evident in its acceptance of several bilateral trade-related demands made by Trump. The government must strengthen the domestic market through a broad-based expansion of demand. India’s abundant human resources must be harnessed to their full potential.

A.G. Rajmohan, Andhra Pradesh

Sir — The Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, signed by Donald Trump, carries a greater degree of legal authority. Indian exports to the US will become too uncompetitive should these new tariffs come to pass. Russian crude accounted for over 51% of India’s oil imports in July as supplies through the Strait of Hormuz remain constrained. India will have to chivvy countries such as Oman to hasten their expansion of alternative ports. India’s ability to secure a low rate will be a true test of the friendship between Narendra Modi and Trump.

Sir — The recent law signed by Donald Trump grants the US discretionary powers to impose country-specific tariffs of up to 100%. India, which sourced approximately 30% of its crude oil imports from Russia in 2025, is a direct target of these measures. Since the tariffs would apply to Indian exports to the US, the economic consequences could extend to exporters, refinery margins, the rupee and the trade balance.

For India, it is a tough balancing act — to protect strategic autonomy in energy procurement while demonstrating credible, time‑bound diversification and robust compliance practices coupled with aggressive export‑market diversification and diplomatic outreach to insulate the broader US-India trade relationship.

Sir — There was a time when life was slow-paced, rhythmic and largely dependent on nature. Today, it is fast, hectic and technology-driven. Students once relied on books, teachers and libraries; smartphones now place limitless information at their fingertips. Yet information and knowledge are not the same thing. Competition, coaching and comparisons can take away the joy of learning. A poor examination result does not mean failure in life. The professional world offers greater choices but also greater uncertainty and pressure. Men share more household responsibilities, while women have gained freedom yet still carry the burden at home. Friendship, love and marriage have changed too: a friend far away can be reached instantly, and young people have greater freedom to choose a partner. But screens cannot replace human connection and instant replies have diminished the beauty of waiting.

Entertainment and food offer countless choices, though families watch separate screens and eat without the connection among food, seasons and festivals. The past had fewer opportunities but often more leisure. We should retain its patience, warmth and contentment while embracing freedom, scientific temper and technology. A beautiful life makes room for progress, relationships and time together.

Shibaji Roy Choudhuri, Calcutta

Sir — The actor, Mithu Mukherjee, is no longer with us. Her performances in a series of films in the 1970s, including Swayamsiddha , Marjina Abdulla and Mouchak , remain etched in the memories of cinephiles. Just as she secured a lasting place in the hearts of audiences, she quietly withdrew from the world of cinema. She worked alongside stars such as Uttam Kumar, Sabitri Chatterjee and Ranjit Mallick. “ Besh korechi prem korechi ”, the song which was picturised on her, became an expression of youthful romance in the 1970s.

Deba Prasad Bhattacharya, Calcutta

Sir — It is heartbreaking to learn of the passing of Mithu Mukherjee, the quintessential girl-next-door figure of Bengali and Hindi cinema, who embodied the charm of the 1970s. Expressive, spirited, and effortless, she rose to stardom after debuting in the 1971 Bengali film, Shesh Parbo . She had no artificial mannerisms associated with screen performances. Although audiences remember her effervescence, her abilities as an actor deserve equal recognition.

Sir — Mithu Mukherjee passed away at 71. Although she withdrew from the limelight following the 1990 film, Ashrita , her roles remain cherished by cinephiles.

editorials.title: Geography of growth
editorials.passage:
The ministry of statistics and programme implementation's recently released Uniform Guidelines for the Compilation of District Domestic Product (DDP) has largely been seen as a statistical exercise. That interpretation misses the larger significance. The guidelines recognise that India's next development challenge is no longer measuring growth alone. It is understanding the geography of growth.

For decades, gross state domestic product has been the principal lens through which India's economic performance has been assessed. It remains indispensable for fiscal transfers, macroeconomic planning and inter-state comparisons. Yet it tells policymakers remarkably little about the spatial distribution of growth within states. A rapidly growing state economy may coexist with districts that remain economically stagnant. Conversely, a state with moderate aggregate growth may be witnessing a wider spread of productive activity across its districts.

This distinction is becoming increasingly important. Nearly half of India's GDP is generated by just five states. Within them, economic activity is even more concentrated. Around 85% of national GDP and 87% of exports originate from roughly 100 of India's nearly 750 districts. India's economy is no longer organised around states. It is increasingly organised through clusters, corridors and cities that cut across administrative averages that state-level statistics cannot fully capture.

This is precisely where DDP becomes an instrument of better public policy. Much of the discussion around DDP assumes that district estimates should closely mirror aggregate GSDP. That expectation is misplaced. A divergence between the two is not necessarily a statistical flaw. From a policymaker's perspective, it may be the most valuable information the data can reveal.

Consider two states that both record 8% GSDP growth. In the first, growth is concentrated in three metropolitan districts. In the second, manufacturing, services and agricultural productivity expand across a much broader set of districts. Aggregate statistics would treat both states as equally successful. Development policy should not. One reflects concentrated prosperity. The other reflects dispersed opportunity.

This matters because governments rarely implement policy at the level of state aggregates. Industrial corridors, logistics parks, employment programmes, skilling initiatives and infrastructure investments are designed and executed in districts. Identifying districts that generate growth, transmit it or remain excluded from regional transformation is thus essential for more efficient public investment.

The significance of DDP extends beyond economic accounting. It marks a broader shift towards place-based policymaking. Recent improvements in labour force surveys, household consumption data and enterprise surveys have steadily made India's statistical system more granular. District Domestic Product completes that evolution by making local economies visible.

DDP is not a measure of welfare; nor should it replace GDP or GSDP. District accounts serve a different purpose. They reveal patterns of concentration, diffusion and exclusion that aggregate numbers are designed to average out. India's aspiration of becoming a developed economy by 2047 will depend not only on sustaining high growth but also on ensuring that growth is geographically broad-based.

Tarun Kumar is a Public Policy Researcher with the School of Public Policy and Governance, TISS Hyderabad. Ashmita Mitra is a Master’s Candidate at the Jindal School of Government & Public Policy, Haryana

editorials.title: Language test: Editorial on Hindi, linguistic identity and Tamil Nadu's resistance
editorials.passage:
Is opposition to the teaching of a particular language an issue of education alone, or is its reach deeper and wider? The Tamil Nadu government’s petition to the Supreme Court to withdraw the Madras High Court’s order to identify land in each district for the building of Jawahar Navodaya Vidyalayas — these are under the aegis of the Central government — has been refused. The state believes that the three-language policy of these Central schools is a ‘backdoor’ way to introduce Hindi. However, the Supreme Court asked Tamil Nadu to get over its anti-Hindi mindset; it cannot be that Hindi will not be taught on the soil of the state. The state should not alienate Delhi and “vice versa”. The Supreme Court’s vision seems to be of a cooperative federalism; to the state counsel’s argument that the federal structure allows the state’s own laws and policies, the court said that this was a unitary government with a federal structure. The language issue should be resolved through dialogue with the Centre. But the matter at hand is complex. The state sees the three-language policy as “fundamentally incompatible” with the state law, the Tamil Nadu Tamil Learning Act, 2006. Moreover, Tamil Nadu’s political and social opposition to Hindi has a long history; it considers Hindi a threat to its distinctive identity and linguistic autonomy. This is allied to the idea of language as a fundamental right, an argument that the state counsel used.

Tamil Nadu’s opposition to Navodaya Vidyalayas has brought out a tension between unitary governance and the federal structure. That it centres on language is especially important in a multilingual country. Education policy, the right to choose a language, and the approach to federalism are all linked in this case. The state’s argument that the Navodaya scheme was an optional policy — education being on the concurrent list, a state could refuse the policies it disagreed with — was evidently not considered comprehensive by the court. Neither was the implicit idea that a state could teach whichever language it preferred because language was a fundamental right. Although there is no separate right enshrined under right to language, there are a number of language-related rights, such as the right to conserve a particular language spoken by any section of citizens. The court’s view of federalism was a broad one: without cooperation the federal structure would disintegrate. The politics of cooperation, however, is rarely smooth, and it is to be hoped that it does not disguise the operations of power.

editorials.title: Two fronts: Editorial on reservation, caste tensions and the BJP’s electoral balancing act
editorials.passage:
One of the principal pillars of the Bharatiya Janata Party’s electoral success in recent years has been its ability to forge and then consolidate a rainbow social coalition that features upper castes, scheduled castes, Dalit constituencies and the other backward classes. Hindutva’s magnetism has served as an umbrella to bring together social constituencies that are not only disparate but also often mutually competing groups. Data suggest that in the 2024 general election, the BJP dominated the vote share among upper castes while registering only a slight dip in its hold among SCs. But is this electorally productive pyramid now under structural strain? The Union health minister, J.P. Nadda, has had to engage — twice in recent days — with upper caste groups protesting against reservations as well as the University Grants Commission’s equity rules that, the protesters allege, discriminate against them. Mr Nadda’s intervention is obviously tied to the BJP’s poll math in election-bound Uttar Pradesh. But what can make this a delicate balancing act is the corresponding rhetoric arising from the SCs, OBCs and even scheduled tribes. They have warned against any weakening of the protections, some of which are constitutionally-mandated. Already, Akhilesh Yadav of the Samajwadi Party, the BJP’s principal rival in UP, is pushing ahead with what he claims is the alliance of the marginalised.

Politics is not the only prism that can be used to examine the emerging fault line. It has significant social and moral dimensions. It appears that the republic’s tryst with equality, a tryst written in blood and toil, is coming under renewed strain. The moral and, hence, constitutional rationale of reservation is unimpeachable. Only a polity stripped of conscience would want the marginalised — the Mahatma’s ‘last person in the line’ — to remain yoked to the mantle of discrimination. But India’s economic cleavages — joblessness, disruptions in the labour market, the State’s withering as a welfarist entity — and that other vector, electoral populism, are increasingly piling pressure on the nation’s conscience and moral fabric. The Congress, in its heyday, had faced a similar quandary and, ultimately, lost its near-monopoly on both upper castes and disadvantaged segments. It remains to be seen whether the BJP, today’s dominant political force, survives the fate of its rival.

editorials.title: Why precision is sharpening Indian manufacturing
editorials.passage:
In 1953, Bengaluru had a factory that produced almost nothing that people could use directly. Hindustan Machine Tools, or HMT, was established with a deceptively ambitious purpose. It would manufacture the ‘mother machines’ needed to build a modern industrial India. Lathes, milling machines and gear shapers were not products most Indians needed to buy; they were the machines for industrial production.

And then came watches. In 1961, HMT established the first watch factory in Bengaluru with Japanese watchmaker Citizen. It had to absorb the technology of mass-producing microscopic components. By 1975, the factory was making mainsprings, hairsprings and shock absorbers in-house, giving it control over the entire process.

The machine tools taught India to make machines with precision; watchmaking pushed that precision into a much smaller world. The industry changed. The discipline did not.

Capability rarely travels in a straight line, moving through people, suppliers, apprenticeships and manufacturing culture, rather than documented lineage. What HMT helped establish was more durable: the idea that precision could become transferable. That capability is visible today across India’s manufacturing ecosystem, in specialised materials, aerospace, defence and advanced engineering, accumulated and recombined, rather than passed down in an unbroken line.

Titan took the opposite route: its precision-engineering arm grew out of watchmaking, and now builds machine tools and aerospace and defence components. The direction hardly matters; the discipline does. Ethereal Machines, based in Bengaluru, is an instructive example. Founded in 2014 by college classmates Kaushik Mudda and Navin Jain to make more precisely cut parts for their own projects, it went on to build indigenous multi-axis CNC platforms, winning a CES Best of Innovation award in 2018. It now runs a machining-as-a-service model for aerospace, medical devices and electronics.

Mudda observes: “My conviction has always been that India has never lacked the engineering talent for advanced manufacturing, only the industrial capability to match it. Ethereal exists to close that gap.” Accurate Engineering Company in Pune illustrates the complementary capability of precision measurement. Established in 1963 by the late Vilasrao Salunkhe to manufacture measuring instruments and gauges, it built decades of expertise in dimensional metrology. Under his son, Vikram, the MD, that legacy continues into digital, shop-floor measurement systems.

Salunkhe emphasises: “AI cannot predict what the factory has never connected. The real promise of AI in precision engineering is not better inspection. It is a factory that increasingly knows the quality of what it is making before the inspection room has to tell it.” This is capability migration. Over time it compounds.

It is worth being precise about what precision actually means. Often reduced to a tight tolerance on a drawing, precision understates what a company has really learned when it can manufacture a demanding component.

It has learned to control a process end to end, qualifying suppliers, managing variation and documenting every step: organisational capabilities that take years to build and only months to redeploy once embedded. A precision manufacturer is, therefore, not merely selling a component: it is selling confidence that the component will be right, every time. That matters as India moves into aerospace, semiconductor equipment and medical devices where failure is unacceptable.

Precision itself is no longer a static discipline. For decades, it meant holding a tolerance and proving it through inspection. AI and digital sensing are shifting that towards prediction: software that flags a process drifting out of specification before a defective part is made. Ethereal’s shift to machining-as-a-service and Accurate’s move into digital, shop-floor measurement are early signs of this. Companies that treat precision as fixed, once earned and simply maintained, may find a purely mechanical definition of the term no longer sufficient to compete.

India’s first manufacturing story was written in the language of cost. That story is not finished, but it is no longer sufficient: the more interesting transition underway is from cost to trust. A global customer does not place a demanding, failure-intolerant component with a supplier merely because it is cheap, but because the supplier has proven, audit after audit, that it can deliver the same result under pressure with traceability and consistency.

Trust, therefore, is not a soft attribute, but an industrial capability, measurable through qualification cycles, audits and how much responsibility a customer transfers to a supplier. There is, however, a warning here: India cannot become merely the world’s precision-machining workshop; precision must become a bridge to innovation.

Indian auto component companies remain markedly less R&D-intensive than global peers, a recent Goldman Sachs analysis notes. Government data put India’s R&D spend at just 0.83 per cent of GDP in 2023-24, well below the 2-4.5 per cent typical of innovation-led economies, though the private industry’s share crossed 50 per cent for the first time that year.

Indian companies must continuously renew their capabilities through R&D, tooling and digital manufacturing, not simply deploy them efficiently. The ambition cannot be to make someone else’s component more cheaply; it must eventually be to own the process and help define the next generation of the product.

That is where manufacturing capability becomes technological capability and technological capability becomes strategic capability.

We tend to ask which sectors India should promote next — aerospace, semiconductors, defence or electronics. The more fundamental question is which capabilities India should deliberately accumulate, knowing they may outlive whichever sector happens to be relevant when they are built.

Precision is one such capability, alongside metrology, tooling, systems engineering and process automation. None of them respect industry boundaries; they can be recombined. A country does not become industrially sophisticated by having factories in many sectors, but when capabilities developed in one make it easier to enter the next.

HMT’s mother machines were built to make the machines that would build modern India. Decades later, precision capabilities developed in automotive, watchmaking, machining and metrology are finding applications in aerospace, defence and semiconductor equipment. The products and the industries will continue to change; what matters is whether the capability beneath them continues to deepen.

India does not need to be good at everything; it needs to become exceptionally good at capabilities the world finds hard to substitute and transfer them faster than others.

Factories manufacture products. Great industries manufacture capabilities. And, capabilities, once genuinely earned, can become the foundation for industries that did not exist when they were first learned.

Vipin Sondhi is an Independent Director and Former MD & CEO of Ashok Leyland and JCB India; G Sundararaman is the Chief Scientist and Head of Wipro Research. Views expressed are personal

editorials.title: Will Pakistan fight for Saudi Arabia?
editorials.passage:
Pakistan could hardly have dreamt when it signed the tripartite Makkah Defence Pact that it could be called on to honour its commitments barely six weeks later.

Yemen’s Houthis have emerged much stronger, seizing major stretches of the Red Sea coastline and pushing towards the Bab al-Mandab strait, a crucial shipping chokepoint. Now they’re firing ballistic missiles and attack drones at Saudi Arabia, including attacks on Riyadh and the kingdom’s vital Red Sea oil infrastructure at Yanbu. On Saturday, a missile aimed at Riyadh was intercepted, while a fire erupted near King Khalid International Airport. The Houthis also claimed an attack on an Aramco facility at Yanbu.

Under the Makkah pact, an armed attack on any one of Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkiye is to be seen as an attack on all. The pact was presented as a collective defence arrangement to deter external aggression.

With the ink barely dry, will Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman call on his two new allies to honour the pledge?

For Pakistan, it’s the ultimate tightrope walk. On one side is its defence deal with Saudi Arabia, to which it has long provided training and security help. Defence Minister Khawaja Asif has said an attack on Saudi Arabia could activate it, while military spokesman Lieutenant-General Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry has said Pakistan stands “physically” and diplomatically with Riyadh.

But Pakistan has presented itself as a peacemaker in the wider Middle East conflict. Field Marshal Asim Munir has made numerous trips to Tehran as Islamabad tries to help end the war.

Complicating things is that the Saudis and Iranians are arch-enemies, and Iran has long backed the Houthis.

It puts Pakistan in an awkward position. The Houthis have amassed some 100,000 fighters and captured strategic territory around the Red Sea. Pakistan faces the prospect of defending Saudi territory against an Iran-backed movement while simultaneously trying to keep diplomatic channels to Tehran open. The Houthis have become so strong that questions are now being asked about whether Saudi Arabia can withstand the assault.

The oil-rich kingdom was created in 1932, and huge oil reserves were soon discovered. Ibn Saud created the new kingdom by bringing together 22 tribes. Now those tribal links could be under strain from the Houthi onslaught.

When Saudi Arabia was formed, it also seized three territories that had been part of Yemen. On Tuesday, Saudi Arabia issued an alert for Najran province, near the Yemeni border, without specifying why.

Then there’s Mohammed bin Salman, or MBS, the kingdom’s de facto ruler while his father remains king. In 2017, MBS arrested top princes and wealthy businessmen, refusing to release them until they handed over vast sums. Some detainees alleged torture, and the episode left deep resentment. MBS has also seized huge swathes of tribal land for his overweening mega-projects, stoking further anger. Many princes and tribal leaders may hope the ageing king will sideline MBS and choose another prince to rule.

The Saudis are also at odds with the UAE. In Yemen, the two Gulf states have backed different sides, creating mutual ill-will. The UAE is considered closer to Israel. Both Gulf states are playing political games abroad and in the larger region. Saudi Arabia is striving to bring peace to Sudan while the UAE has been accused of interfering in African countries. Algeria recently blocked overflights by Emirati aircraft because it believes the Gulf state is backing Morocco’s claims against Algeria in the Sahel region.

The wider point is that the Gulf is a relatively recent political construct, assembled largely in the first half of the 20th century. These states then relied heavily on the US for military backing and security.

But Washington has made clear it can’t handle another war on top of the Iran conflict. Trump is said to have rejected requests from MBS to bomb the Houthis. The Houthis have therefore managed something once almost impossible: forcing Saudi Arabia to look beyond its American security umbrella towards regional alliances.

Which brings the crisis back to Pakistan. It has just signed a collective security pact with Saudi Arabia and Turkiye while trying to mediate between Iran and the US.

Now the two roles are colliding.

If Riyadh asks Pakistan to activate the Makkah pact, Islamabad will have to decide how far it will go in defending Saudi Arabia against the Houthis while maintaining its carefully cultivated ties with Iran, with which Pakistan shares a 400-mile border.

It may be a case of being careful what you wish for. Pakistan has long wanted a larger Middle East role. Now, it may be discovering that becoming a regional power-broker can come with a very high price.

editorials.title: Easing funding for coops
editorials.passage:
The NCDC Amendment Bill, 2026 seeks to update the institutional and financial framework of the National Cooperative Development Corporation (NCDC) in line with the changing requirements of India’s cooperative sector. One of its significant features is the widening of institutional channels for cooperative development.

Many organisations supporting cooperatives are not themselves registered as cooperative societies, and under the existing framework NCDC may face limitations in directly financing such institutions even when their activities substantially benefit cooperatives. The proposed provision enabling NCDC to finance “any entity engaged in cooperative development”, subject to prescribed conditions, can address this institutional gap and facilitate a wider ecosystem involving infrastructure providers, technology institutions, processing organisations, marketing agencies and other specialised entities.

The Bill also seeks to facilitate faster and more direct financial assistance by permitting NCDC to provide loans and grants directly to eligible entities engaged in cooperative development. This could reduce procedural delays and support time-sensitive projects relating to technology, infrastructure, processing, storage, market linkages and value-chain development. Greater flexibility in financing is particularly relevant as cooperatives are increasingly diversifying into processing, branding, logistics, digital services, marketing and other modern business activities. Faster and more flexible finance can contribute to quicker project implementation, provided that appropriate appraisal, monitoring and risk-management systems are maintained.

Another important proposal is to permit NCDC, with the Centre’s approval of the Central Government, to participate in the share capital of cooperative societies or entities engaged in cooperative development. This can potentially strengthen the capital base of institutions that require long-term financial support beyond conventional borrowing. However, equity participation also exposes public funds to investment and business risks, making due diligence, valuation, investment limits, risk assessment, performance monitoring and appropriate exit mechanisms important. The proposed expansion of “foodstuffs” to include other food items notified by the Centre Central Government, together with removal of the geographical restriction relating to industrial goods, may further facilitate diversification, value addition and greater cooperative participation in modern supply chains.

The offered power to collect and share credit information with the Reserve Bank of India and other notified financial institutions can strengthen credit appraisal, reduce information asymmetry and support more responsible lending and risk management. Taken together, these provisions have the potential to enable financing across the cooperative value chain, from production and processing to storage, marketing and supporting infrastructure, with possible benefits for Primary Agricultural Cooperative Credit Societies (PACS), cooperative marketing societies, processing cooperatives and other grassroots institutions. The broader approach is also consistent with the expansion and diversification of India’s cooperative sector, particularly following the establishment of the Ministry of Cooperation in 2021, and provides a rationale for updating legislation originally enacted in 1962.

At the same time, the wider NCDC mandate raises concerns regarding the potential expansion of beneficiaries beyond cooperative societies. Although the Statement of “Objects and Reasons” indicates that cooperatives will remain the primary beneficiaries, clear eligibility criteria and safeguards are essential to prevent disproportionate diversion of resources to non-cooperative entities. The framework should also ensure adequate access and priority for PACS and other grassroots cooperatives, which may face capacity constraints. Expanded powers should be accompanied by stronger accountability, transparent reporting on beneficiaries and financial assistance, outcome-based performance assessment, and effective coordination with State cooperative departments, cooperative banks and other institutions. Simplification should promote efficiency without excluding relevant stakeholders.

The implementation framework should therefore clearly define an “entity engaged in cooperative development”, establish objective eligibility criteria, preserve cooperative societies as the primary beneficiaries, provide appropriate priority to grassroots institutions, and prescribe safeguards for equity participation and beneficiary selection.

A clear “cooperative-benefit test” would be particularly valuable: financing of a non-cooperative entity should be justified by identifiable and measurable benefits to cooperative societies and their members. The guiding principle should therefore be: wider powers for NCDC, but with stronger safeguards to ensure that cooperative societies and their members remain the primary beneficiaries.

The writer is Director, Institute of Cooperative Management, Madurai; (An Institution of National Council for Cooperative Training – New Delhi) – Ministry of Cooperation, Government of India
