editorials.title: Why it’s time to scrap dollar billing for local SEZ deals
editorials.passage:
India’s special economic zones were built on a simple export logic: transactions with a customer outside the zone, in the domestic tariff area (DTA), must earn foreign exchange for the country. That rule still applies to services, even though it was relaxed for goods long ago. A software company, or a defence contractor sitting inside an SEZ, selling to an Indian client a few kilometres away in the same city, is currently required to bill that client in dollars.

The Indian buyer must first purchase foreign currency from an authorised dealer bank, paying a commission, and the SEZ unit must then convert those dollars back into rupees, paying another commission, for a transaction that never actually leaves the country. Public sector undertakings in defence, space and aerospace, which rely on specialised maintenance and engineering services from SEZ-based firms, have complained for years that this pushes up costs without any benefit to the exchequer.

The Commerce Department has circulated a draft Cabinet note, proposing an amendment to Section 2(z) of the SEZ Act, 2005, the provision that governs how services must be paid for. The change would allow SEZ units to receive rupee payments for services rendered to DTA customers, bringing services in line with the treatment already available for goods. Officials are also working to align the statutory definition of a service with the one used under the Goods and Services Tax law.

The sectors expected to benefit the most are IT, IT-enabled services, defence, aerospace, engineering, maintenance, and repair and overhaul work, where an Indian unit can often complete a task in about a week, compared with over a year for a foreign vendor. The note is currently under inter-ministerial consultation among Commerce, Finance, and the Reserve Bank before it goes to the Cabinet.

If cleared, the amendment removes the pain point for the services sector and makes SEZ units more attractive to local vendors, particularly for government departments reluctant to handle the paperwork and costs of foreign-currency billing. It also arrives at a moment when several IT firms have been reconsidering their SEZ presence following the withdrawal of earlier Income Tax incentives, so rupee billing could be one more reason to stay put. The grey areas are just as real. SEZs are legally treated as territory outside India for many purposes, and that fiction underpins their customs and tax privileges .

Loosening the foreign exchange requirement for services, without an equally tight definition of what constitutes a domestic transaction, risks blurring the line that regulators have historically guarded closely. How tightly the final rules are drawn will depend on the balance between a Commerce Ministry keen on ease of doing business and a Finance Ministry watchful of revenue leakage.

A harmonised definition of services across the SEZ Act and the GST law is the right starting point, paired with sector-specific guidance, since the needs of a defence contractor billing a public sector client are not the same as those of an IT firm billing a private one. The RBI and authorised dealer banks will need a clear operating framework for rupee settlement so that banks are not left to interpret an ambiguous rule on their own.

This amendment need not be seen only as a narrow fix to a billing anomaly. It could be a first step towards a broader rethink of how SEZs, designed for a world of export-led growth, now fit into an economy where the domestic market is often the bigger opportunity.

Saravanan is Professor of Finance and Accounting at IIM-Tiruchirappalli; Williams is the Head of India at Sernova Financial

editorials.title: India Inc’s price dilemma
editorials.passage: By K Ravichandran For India Inc, the challenge in FY27 may not simply be higher input costs, but how much of those costs can be passed on without weakening demand. Companies are entering a period in which price increases can protect margins and revenues but also put pressure on volumes. The result could be a widening divergence between headline revenue growth and the underlying quality of corporate earnings. The Q1 results offered a glimpse of this. India Inc’s revenues grew by 21.3% year-on-year (y-o-y), supported by commodity- and bullion-price-led value inflation and volume growth in select sectors. However, operating profit margins contracted by 171 basis points (bps). Excluding oil and gas, aggregate operating margins were more resilient, improving marginally to 18.1% from 17.9% a year earlier. ALSO READAn Arctic security bargain Revenue growth is expected to remain healthy at around 13-15% in Q2 FY27, although moderating from the unusually strong performance in Q1. Cost inflation-led growth is likely to sustain, but volumetric consumption growth could moderate as companies raise prices to offset higher raw material, energy, labour, and freight costs. Operating profit margins could contract by 100-150 bps y-o-y in Q2 FY27, as elevated input costs continue to weigh on profitability. While external uncertainties persist, attention has increasingly shifted to emerging domestic risks. El Niño has added a fresh layer of uncertainty to India’s macroeconomic outlook, mainly through its implications for the southwest monsoon. A subpar monsoon could disrupt rural demand, impacting FMCG companies’ revenues, and its impact could extend beyond the farm sector. Deficient rainfall can push up food inflation even as it compresses rural incomes, both of which directly influence consumption demand. Other sectors with significant rural exposure, including tractors, two-wheelers, and fertilisers, may face volume pressures. Weaker farm cash flows could also result in subdued credit demand and increased stress in agricultural and microfinance portfolios. This makes the ability of companies to pass on higher costs increasingly important. Pricing actions can provide some protection to margins, but the benefits may come with a lag. For consumption-oriented sectors, an abrupt increase in prices could hit demand and competitive positioning. Cost optimisation, productivity improvements, and operating efficiencies could consequently become as important as pricing power in determining profitability. Oil refining companies are likely to continue facing pressure from under-recoveries on petroleum products and thinner marketing margins. Aviation, automobiles, FMCG, cement, and other energy-intensive sectors are also exposed to higher crude oil and derivative prices, palm oil, coal, and other inputs, as well as the consequent rise in freight and packaging costs. For some sectors, however, the ability to raise prices could provide a partial cushion. FMCG companies, for instance, are seeing healthy volume growth, supported by improving domestic consumption, but higher logistics and packaging costs, along with more expensive imported inputs like palm oil, are expected to weigh on margins. Price revisions could partly offset this pressure, although companies may have to stagger such increases to avoid affecting demand and competitive positioning. The automobile sector presents a similar balancing act. Demand has benefitted from GST reforms and new model launches, but the high base, a potentially weak monsoon, and higher fuel prices could moderate growth. A sustained rise in petrol and diesel prices could weigh heavily on price-sensitive two-wheeler and entry-level passenger-vehicle segments, while higher logistics costs could put pressure on OEMs and auto-component margins. Some sectors are better positioned to withstand the margin pressure. Metals and mining firms are supported by favourable commodity realisations, while upstream oil producers benefit from higher crude prices. Telecom operators and select utilities are also relatively better placed, supported by operating leverage or cost-pass-through mechanisms. Export-oriented sectors like textiles and auto components could benefit from better realisations arising from rupee depreciation, although their performance will remain contingent on global demand. Some export-oriented firms are likely to see a one-time earnings support in Q2 FY27 from refunds of US tariffs paid earlier. While domestic consumption-oriented sectors like automobiles, retail, consumer durables, and hospitality are expected to remain better placed, persistent weakness in global demand and the transformation of the technology sector could weigh on export-oriented businesses. Domestic demand itself can’t be taken for granted. Retail inflation is also expected to edge higher over the next few quarters, potentially constraining discretionary spending, making it harder for firms to rely entirely on price increases to protect margins. Over the past few years, corporate balance sheets have been deleveraged, providing a cushion against cyclical fluctuations in demand. The financial sector’s strength, with comfortable asset quality and capitalisation levels, should also provide the capacity to absorb stress while supporting credit growth. ALSO READWho guards governance? The resilience of corporate credit profiles is important in assessing the impact of margin compression. Despite the expected moderation in operating margins, interest coverage is projected to remain resilient supported by stable funding costs. This suggests the current margin pressure need not immediately translate into widespread credit stress. The push for infrastructure development and clean energy is expected to anchor investment activity, even as private sector capex recovery remains gradual. Select segments of manufacturing, including defence, electronics manufacturing, and electric mobility, along with power equipment, real estate, and data centres, are emerging as areas of private investment. Nevertheless, a broad-based revival in private investment is likely to remain contingent on greater clarity around global and domestic conditions. For India Inc, the coming quarters may be less about the headline pace of revenue growth and more about its quality. If inflation continues to support topline growth while input costs remain elevated, the ability to convert revenues into operating profits will increasingly depend on pricing power, cost efficiency, and the resilience of demand. The writer is Executive Vice President & Chief Ratings Officer, ICRA. Disclaimer: The views expressed are the author's own and do not reflect the official policy or position of Financial Express.

editorials.title: Chips, then chokepoints
editorials.passage: The semiconductor journey is beginning to look like a policy bet that is paying off. Semicon 1.0 was meant to get the industry started, and it has done that with a scale of investment that would have been difficult to imagine a few years ago. Twelve projects with investment commitments of more than Rs 1.64 lakh crore have been approved, covering fabs, compound semiconductors, and packaging, with five units now in commercial production. Chip design has also moved forward, with 24 projects approved and more than 100,000 engineers getting access to advanced design tools. The response from industry at Semicon India, which concluded last week, reinforces that the pace and direction are on the right lines. Investment commitments of around Rs 1 lakh crore under Semicon 2.0, spanning equipment, materials, gases, chemicals, and other parts of the supply chain, point to an ecosystem that is beginning to widen. Prime Minister Narendra Modi described the transition as moving from files to factories, while Information Technology Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw said that the next phase is about building the complete ecosystem. ALSO READIndia Inc’s price dilemma That is precisely what Semicon 2.0 is meant to do. With a much larger Rs 127,500-crore outlay, the programme goes deeper into equipment and materials, advanced packaging, design, R&D, and talent. This matters because a semiconductor industry cannot be built around a handful of fabs. The growing interest among global companies in these parts of the chain suggests that the opportunity is beginning to extend well beyond fabrication and packaging. If Semicon 1.0 was about creating capacity, the second phase is about creating the depth that can sustain it. But the road ahead may not be as straightforward as the progress so far suggests. Semiconductor history offers reason for caution. The industry has repeatedly been shaped not just by economics and technology but by trade policy, strategic alliances, and geopolitical rivalry. The US-Japan semiconductor conflict of the 1980s, followed by the emergence of South Korea and Taiwan as major manufacturing centres, shows how the geography of chips can change when technology and strategic interests intersect. Today, companies are looking to diversify concentrated supply chains and build trusted alternatives, creating an opening for newer manufacturing locations. But as capabilities deepen, the possibility that geopolitical interests could seek to slow a competitor's rise cannot be dismissed. China’s restrictions on critical minerals, including rare earths, have already demonstrated how control over an upstream input can disrupt industries across countries. Semiconductor supply chains have even more strategic chokepoints, from equipment and materials to technology and intellectual property. ALSO READThe shifting sands This is why the next phase of the semiconductor strategy has to be about more than attracting investment. It must anticipate the possibility that the global environment could become less accommodating as capabilities deepen. That does not mean trying to make everything at home or withdrawing from global supply chains. It means reducing the number of points at which the ecosystem can be vulnerable to disruption, while building relationships with multiple trusted partners. The opportunity has been created partly by the fragmentation of global supply chains. But the same forces could eventually make the emergence of another major semiconductor hub more contested. The gains made through Semicon 1.0 and the momentum of Semicon 2.0 are significant. The task now is to ensure that the ecosystem being built is deep and diversified enough to withstand the geopolitical pressures that may accompany its success.

editorials.title: It’s easy to ignore the Lib Dems, but they could soon hold the balance of power
editorials.passage:
N o politician craves obscurity, but it is better to be unknown than despised. That is consolation for Liberal Democrats , gathered in Brighton for their annual conference, fretting about Ed Davey’s low profile and wondering whether a more prominent leader would hoist their flagging poll ratings.

Renewal by decapitation is a concept that has succeeded twice this parliament for other parties. Labour’s fortunes were transformed when Andy Burnham entered No 10. The Greens enjoyed a polling surge last year when Zack Polanski was elected leader. In the fidgety culture of British politics, Davey’s six-year reign feels like an aeon . But the experience of other parties has little to teach the Lib Dems.

Keir Starmer didn’t suffer from underexposure. The country watched a showcase of his abilities and didn’t like what it saw. Polanski’s talent for harvesting clicks on social media has expanded his audience, especially among younger voters, but the Green leader hasn’t shown that he can sustain that interest. Increased scrutiny may not do him any favours. The chart mapping his favourability ratings since taking the job shows a stable core of fans beneath a steadily rising line of disapproval, suggesting that, outside a Green comfort zone, the more people see of Polanski, they less they like. The equivalent picture for Davey tells a story of flat indifference.

Voters don’t have a clear sense of what the Lib Dem leader stands for , but they don’t feel threatened by him, which is an underrated value in a leader whose prospects depend on tactical voting. His supporters aren’t relaxed about a polling slump but they argue that the party’s tally of seats in parliament and on local councils is evidence that more has gone right than wrong in recent years.

They have a point. There are 72 Lib Dem MPs – a record high – and reasons to expect that number to grow at the next election. The party prides itself on tenacious incumbency, digging in deep and fortifying each seat with local activism. Lib Dems are resented by rivals for the same reason, compared to cockroaches for their stubborn resistance to removal. Those tactics can’t protect a popular local candidate if a national tide turns against the party, as happened in 2015 when the Lib Dems were crushed almost to death by the weight of amassed resentment over their coalition collaboration with the Tories. But sometimes the party finds itself swimming with the current.

To the extent that any forecast can reliably be made about Britain’s choppy political waters, it looks likely that a decisive factor at the next general election will be the question of Reform UK’s suitability for power and, assuming he is still the leader, Nigel Farage’s candidacy to be prime minister. The result will then depend on the organisation of tactical anti-Farage voting (and levels of dysfunction in any putative Reform-Conservative pact) at constituency level.

That dynamic can work in Davey’s favour if the question of who is best placed to stop the radical right is unambiguous. Conservatives are the challengers in nearly all of the Lib Dems’ current constituencies and the incumbents in most of the party’s target seats. Given how porous the ideological membrane is between Tories and Reform, Lib-Dem campaigners in key battlegrounds can correctly argue that a vote for Labour or Greens serves only to enable Faragism.

Davey is already building that case. He presents his party’s bloc of MPs as a “ firewall ” to stop British politics being captured by a brand of demagogic nationalism that is inspired by Donald Trump and bankrolled by unsavoury billionaires.

An obvious inference from that position is that Davey would facilitate Burnham staying on in Downing Street in a hung parliament. Speculation on that question, years before an election is even due, is tedious but necessary for the Lib Dems. They find it demeaning to be cast as parliamentary handmaids waiting to serve a grander political master, but at least that status keeps them relevant. Coalition is the mechanism by which Davey can plausibly get manifesto commitments enacted. It is an important point of distinction from what Lib Dems see as sideline pressure-group politics practised by the Greens.

The strategy gets trickier if the Lib Dems already maxed out the anti-rightwing tactical vote in 2024, when there was the pressing matter of a Tory government to evict. Where do they go next?

A suite of victories in that campaign established a base for the party in the “ blue wall ” of affluent southern towns and suburbs. These are places that once dependably voted Tory but where the old allegiance has been sundered by a combination of demographic change (younger voters moving in), rank incompetence (Boris Johnson; Liz Truss) and unhinged Brexit fanaticism.

The cultural shift is not superficial, but nor is it baked in so hard that the Lib Dems can afford to lean too far to the left. Consolidation and growth depend on expansion into the vacant space on the political spectrum where moderate “one nation” Tories once dwelt and that Kemi Badenoch is not reclaiming.

That risks causing discomfort to Lib Dems in the party’s orthodox social-democratic tradition, or who campaign in seats where the opposition is Labour. They want to compete in radical colours – a reddish shade of orange, not a pale orangey-blue. They don’t see themselves as a party of the centre-right.

Davey has a balance to strike . He needs to signal progressive credentials to reassure tactical voters and Lib Dem activists that his anti-Farage firewall will be suitably robust. He also needs to consolidate and expand his support among former Tory voters who might be liberal on social matters but are still classically conservative on the economy.

His conference speech on Tuesday was crafted with those twin tracks in mind. He led with impassioned denunciation of far-right thuggery on British streets, connecting it to Reform’s anti-immigration agenda, but the headline retail offer was a big income tax cut – raising the personal allowance and the 40p threshold. The latter would be a gift to people who, like everyone else, feel squeezed by inflation and stagnant wages but are far from the neediest end of national income distribution.

It is an expensive gamble. In theory, the £17bn cost to the exchequer would be recovered once the British economy was restored to the EU single market and thriving as a result. Spending a reverse-Brexit dividend on tax cuts is a cute political message for middle-class remainers. It wouldn’t pass a Treasury test of fiscal neutrality given the complexity and upfront cost of the accession process.

Davey is prepared to take heat in accusations of sketchy budgeting, verging on denial of fiscal reality, if the row also sheds light on his pro-European, tax-cutting ambition for the benefit of people who care about both of those things.

It is a targeted bet on raising the Lib Dems’ profile with the specific voters who will decide how many seats the party wins. That number can’t be extrapolated from midterm opinion polls.

Local elections next year will give some indication of whether Davey’s method is working. A byelection in a winnable seat may settle Lib Dem nerves. But the plan only comes to fruition as the sum of tactical choices made in polling booths in a general election, once voters confront the prospect of Reform in government.

Right now, it may not be obvious what purpose the Lib Dems serve, but if they hold enough seats to thwart a Faragist majority, their utility to British democracy won’t be in doubt. That is the uncertainty inherent in a firewall. You only find out whether it works when you need it most, and then you don’t get a second chance.

Rafael Behr is a Guardian columnist

editorials.title: Trump invades the UN with a brutish speech
editorials.passage:
E xpectations were low for Donald Trump’s address to the UN on Tuesday, and yet somehow it was even worse than expected. He does not perform well in formal settings, like chambers of government, preferring a blingier room, like Mar-a-Lago, or an outdoor rally. For years, he has made no secret of his hostility to the UN, and the very principles of international order that define it.

In recent years, that hostility has deepened into something more like a full-on assault, with frequent attacks on the international criminal court (perhaps out of fear that he will someday be indicted), on the UN’s climate agenda, and on Unesco (which the US decided to withdraw from in July 2025).

His flamboyant effort to launch a so-called Board of Peace in January (just before launching his war of choice on Iran) was another attack on the UN, which, at times, the president wondered if his new creation might simply replace.

Five months later, it has achieved little in the way of tangible results, except to demand huge sums of money from its small number of member nations, most of which are petrostates. Not one of those states can say that the Middle East is in better shape since the board came into existence, with a crisis that is deepening daily and may engulf Saudi Arabia soon.

But even by Trumpian standards, this was a hollow speech, long on snarling belligerence and short on ideas or policy proposals. The president read robotically from a teleprompter for long stretches, except when he remembered one of the many complaints about the world that he has memorized from his rallies, and a history of grievances that goes back to his rise as a xenophobic developer in the 1980s.

In short, he insulted nearly everyone in the room, from the Middle Eastern countries who are wondering about the validity of US security guarantees, to the European allies he habitually belittles, to Ukraine, whose leader, Volodymyr Zelensky was in the room, undoubtedly wondering why Trump is now asking him to pause his effective strikes on the Russian invader.

A famous episode of Seinfeld introduced “Festivus”, a holiday for the sharing of grievances. It felt like that as Trump outlined his Hobbesian vision of the world, with touches of Rodney Dangerfield added in, from a president who complains endlessly that he gets no respect.

In one stretch, he seemed to be lobbying for a Nobel peace prize while boasting of all the conflicts he has solved, as audience members yawned and checked their phones. He mentioned that these wars had previously been “unendable”, an interesting word that effectively describes two wars today. The Ukraine-Russian war is still going strong despite his frequent promises (including today) to to stop it.

Then, of course, there is the war of choice in Iran that he launched nearly seven months ago. As he has so many times in his social media outbursts, he ranged erratically from threats to “ annihilate the Islamic Republic ” with car-salesman promises to help Iran achieve greatness if they will just agree to work with him. Which, obviously, they will not, as they continue to defy US threats and even to solidify their position (which has improved markedly with Houthi gains in the last two weeks).

Trump insisted that stocks of American weapons are increasing, when all news reports are they are rapidly being depleted .

There was a lengthy assault on climate crisis, claiming (falsely) that the earth’s climate is cooling, and that the science is a hoax when August tied a record for the hottest month ever recorded, and several important science reports in the last week confirmed how dire the situation is. In Tennessee, the temperature on the field of a football game between the Titans and the Philadelphia Eagles reached 157F. Perhaps that is what the president meant when he bragged that the US is the “hottest” country in the world? He may need a new speechwriter – that claim was also made in his 2025 speech to the UN.

Another neologism was “super-intelligence”, or “SI”, a term that the president is hoping will suddenly replace “AI”, much as he tried to rename Lake Ontario and the Gulf of Mexico. Time will tell, but it feels unlikely the new term will stick.

On the eve of an important summit and state dinner with Xi Jinping, this might have been an important moment to stake out ways the US and China might cooperate on AI, to mitigate risks and increase the potential for beneficial research into disease and other problems. That opportunity was not seized.

Other topics that were not addressed included our rapidly deteriorating relationship with Canada , once the US’s greatest ally, and now enraged by Trump’s constant insults. Far from bending Canada to his will, they are achieving the opposite effect, as it always Elbows Up now. It will take years to repair the damage to a vital strategic relationship to the North.

Instead, more attention was paid to Greenland . The president claimed the US would now be enjoying basing rights – which we already enjoy – and he also suggested that foreign adversaries would not be allowed on their bases. That is hardly news – they have never been allowed bases on Greenland.

While discussing his own vision of sovereignty, including his claims to Venezuelan oil, Trump drew from a sordid page of US history, and quoted a corrupt New York politician, William M “Boss” Tweed, to say “to the victor belong the spoils”. Tweed, the leader of Tammany Hall, was later convicted of stealing tens of millions of dollars from the public, and died in jail.

Perhaps the saddest aspect of this speech was its utter lack of American idealism – the very force that led to the UN’s creation. In the 250th year of the United States, there were plenty of themes that might have won over a skeptical audience, but there were no inspiring words about fighting poverty, or reducing nuclear tests or keeping weapons out of space (as John F Kennedy promised in 1963).

Or human rights (introduced as a major theme by Jimmy Carter in 1977), or about reducing tensions with Russia (which Ronald Reagan spoke about in 1988), or the end of the cold war (which George HW Bush celebrated in 1990), or the need to fight terrorism while avoiding Islamophobia (as Bill Clinton explained carefully in 1998).

It was just raw power; and a power that is likely to diminish in the years ahead. The power of persuasion has always been critical to presidents coming into the United Nations. But the United States is now at historically low levels of approval around the world, as measured by the Pew Global Attitudes project, with only 23% of people (across 36 nations) expressing confidence in Trump’s leadership. The number is unlikely to go up after today’s performance.

Ted Widmer, a former White House speechwriter, is the editor of American Speeches, and the recently published The Living Declaration: A Biography of America’s Founding Text, both published by the Library of America

editorials.title: Europe frets about Trump. But soon he could be the least of our problems
editorials.passage:
I addressed a group of more than 100 European ambassadors recently on the big challenges facing the continent this year and next. My main point to these senior diplomats was that, perhaps counterintuitively, Europe’s biggest external challenges over the next 12 months will come from Russia and China, rather than the US.

Europe’s relationship with Trump’s America remains difficult. The US president has weakened confidence in Nato, raised new transatlantic trade tensions and introduced uncertainty into everything from US support for Ukraine to his territorial designs on Greenland. Yet paradoxically, and notwithstanding Trump’s latest tariff threats over the EU’s outreach to Canada, the transatlantic relationship is becoming the more stable part of Europe’s external environment. Not stable, but more stable.

Compared with Russia and China, Europe’s disputes with Washington remain somewhat bounded – and largely negotiable. Ukraine’s rapidly expanding drone capabilities, its military innovation and battlefield experience have made Kyiv a more valuable partner for Washington. US defence companies are also benefiting from Europe’s military support for Ukraine and rearmament against Russia. The US, Denmark and Greenland now say they have struck a deal to allow the US to develop a significant military presence on Greenland. The devil will be in the detail, but they have much stronger incentives to reach an accommodation than to allow the issue to become a lasting source of confrontation.

Trade tensions more broadly will persist, particularly over European regulation of American tech companies. The same is true of Nato, which has lost credibility because of Trump’s frequent admonishments. Nonetheless, these disputes are among countries with deeply interconnected security and economic interests. The risks posed to Europe by Russia and China are more structural – and increasingly point towards escalation.

Russia is becoming more dangerous because it is becoming weaker. The Kremlin is running out of cheap and politically painless ways to finance its war in Ukraine. Its original budget assumptions for 2026 have been overtaken by events. Military spending continues to rise, driven not only by the need for equipment but by the growing cost of recruiting soldiers for the frontline and paying compensation to casualties.

How Vladimir Putin funds his war is now the battlefield behind the battlefield. Further tax increases would damage an economy that, outside the military sector, is approaching recession. Borrowing has become more expensive, while public spending – on everything from schools and hospitals to infrastructure – is being squeezed to preserve the war effort.

Rather than push Putin towards compromise, Russia’s economic challenges are likely, initially at least, to produce the opposite effect. If he expects his economic position to worsen next year, the Kremlin has a powerful incentive to improve its military position now. That means escalation in Ukraine and against Nato. This explains the recent impromptu visit to Moscow by the CIA director, John Ratcliffe.

In Ukraine, Russia is likely to accelerate its mobilisation efforts and engage in heavier attacks on Ukrainian cities and infrastructure, intensifying its efforts to undermine Ukraine’s economy and civilian morale this winter. The coming months will also see an escalation of Russia’s hybrid warfare activity against Nato countries.

China presents a different but equally serious challenge . For years, Europe has debated whether China is competing fairly. That argument is essentially over. A broad consensus now exists that China’s subsidies, industrial overcapacity, undervalued exchange rate and export-led economic model require a political response . The question is no longer whether Europe should defend itself against unfair Chinese competition, but how far it is prepared to go.

Beijing, meanwhile, has reached a very different conclusion. It increasingly sees Europe’s trade-defence measures, industrial policy and economic security agenda as an attempt to constrain China’s growth.

The European commissioner for trade and economic security, Maroš Šefčovič, and his Chinese counterpart, Wang Wentao, met in late June and committed to resolving a number of outstanding issues by October. That may delay confrontation. It is unlikely to avert it.

China is not going to abandon its use of industrial subsidies, the exchange rate or its export-led growth model. These are central features of China’s economic-strategy, and not subject to negotiation. Equally, the EU is not going to retreat from its economic security agenda. The union is developing investment controls, procurement restrictions and new industrial and trade-defence instruments. Although formally country-agnostic, many are clearly directed towards China.

Every European measure to reduce dependence on China is therefore likely to prompt a Chinese response, while every Chinese retaliation will strengthen the political case in Brussels to go further. That makes compromise harder, and escalation between the two sides more likely over the medium term.

The most likely outcome is managed confrontation, rather than a full-scale trade war. The EU will expand targeted restrictions limiting China’s access in additional sectors. China will respond with selective tariffs, procurement barriers, regulatory pressure on European companies and tighter controls on critical minerals. Both sides will try to increase pressure without losing control.

Europe has leverage, too. China remains extraordinarily dependent on access to the EU single market, one of the world’s last large and wealthy export destinations. Europe can withstand coercion – if its governments remain united.

That is why France’s presidential election next year could prove more consequential for Europe than any decision taken in Washington, Moscow or Beijing. Far-right leader Marine Le Pen has a credible path to victory. She is scoring 35% to 38% in first-round polling at present, and is a more formidable candidate than her younger lieutenant, Jordan Bardella, who many assumed would be the Rassemblement National’s candidate in next year’s race. Her prospects will depend heavily on whether France’s fragmented centre can unite behind a single candidate. If it cannot, Le Pen could face the hard-left renegade Jean-Luc Mélenchon in the second round – and would probably win.

A Le Pen presidency would be profoundly disruptive for Europe. She would probably oppose further support for Ukraine, obstruct sanctions against Russia, undermine the bloc’s approach to China and initiate battles with Brussels over Schengen, fiscal rules, electricity pricing and the single market. Her threat to withhold France’s contribution to the EU budget could plunge the union into an unprecedented financial and constitutional crisis.

Europe’s external challenges, while substantial, are manageable. But the decisive variable is Europe itself: whether it can maintain the political coherence required to deal with the US, Russia and China. A Le Pen victory would call that coherence into question, precisely when Europe needs it most.

Mujtaba Rahman is the managing director for Europe at Eurasia Group, a political risk research and consulting firm

editorials.title: How would AI actually ‘kill all humans’? Here are the top five most likely scenarios
editorials.passage:
E arlier this month, artificial intelligence researcher Jacob Coxon resigned from Anthropic after just four months. In an announcement on X, he stated : “The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.”

A senior member of Anthropic’s staff, Evan Hubinger, actually agreed with Coxon, adding he personally thinks the chance of this happening in the next decade is more than 10% .

Understandably, these statements made waves . There’s now lots of talk about slowing down AI research and increasing “ human control ” over the technology.

But how exactly might AI kill us all? There’s no shortage of fantastical scenarios, and most of them involve the concept of “superintelligent” AI – that is, AI that’s more capable than humans.

I’ve distilled these scenarios down to the top five, ordering them roughly from most vague to most precise. And I’d argue the list is also ordered from least to most probable.

AI doomers often justify their concerns by means of an annoying catch-22 paradox: how can we possibly imagine what a superintelligence might do to take out less intelligent beings like us?

We’d have to be superintelligent to predict what a superintelligence would be able to do. It’s like asking your family dog to imagine thermonuclear war.

The good news here is that superintelligence is still perhaps some distance away. Current AI models are really good at solving particular problems, but that’s not the same as being more intelligent than a human in all domains .

However, AI did recently solve one of the seven most challenging maths problems known. It’s apparently closing in on others, which might leave you feeling less optimistic here.

A superintelligent AI would probably be extraordinarily competent at achieving its goals. But it might be indifferent to human survival.

A classic example of such indifference comes from Oxford philosopher Nick Bostrom’s imagined superintelligent AI that has been designed to optimise paperclip production. To produce its preferred form of office supplies, it quickly converts all available matter – including humans, planets and stars – into paperclips.

What we have here is the perfect execution of improperly specified objectives. The AI doesn’t hate humanity; it simply recognises we’re composed of atoms that could be better utilised for paperclips. It’s not personal.

The good news here is that this scenario confuses intelligence with power. A superintelligent AI doesn’t necessarily have the power to achieve its goals. Turning the planet into paperclip factories would require planning permissions.

Even if it got the permissions, building too many paperclip factories would lead to inevitable public outcry. Interest groups would block the proceedings in the courts. Environmental activists would block the bulldozers.

There’s a lot of friction in the world that prevents even the very intelligent from imposing their will on the rest of us. In fact, you could think of datacentres as a current embodiment of the theoretical paperclip scenario. And humans are increasingly pushing back against turning the planet over to datacentres .

Humanity could be killed by a superintelligent AI making and releasing some dangerous new bioweapon into the atmosphere. This is, in fact, one outcome of the AI 2027 scenario by the AI Futures Project, a non-profit dedicated to forecasting the impacts of advanced AI.

This risk was made more concrete last month, when researchers at Stanford University announced they’d used a genetic language AI model to synthesise 16 new viruses.

Worryingly, they just sent the genetic sequences off to a mail-order lab and it sent the viruses back in test tubes. The whole experiment cost a couple of hundred thousand dollars at most.

The good news here is that it’s remarkably hard to kill everyone with a new virus . To do that, you need a virus that’s very transmissible, so it spreads far and wide. But it’s a rule of biology – viruses that spread easily are typically less fatal. By contrast, if a virus is very fatal, transmissibility tends to go down, as most people infected die before there’s time to spread the infection.

Covid killed less than 1% of humanity . The deadliest pandemic in recorded history was the Black Death, when the plague killed more than one-third of Europe’s population in the 14th century. However, even the plague would be much less deadly today due to our increased medical knowledge and better sanitation.

What if AI got into the nuclear command and control chain and started a nuclear war? We’ve come close to nuclear war by mistake several times in the past 50 years.

We’re told that nuclear command and control is completely disconnected from the internet. But, as we saw in 2010, Iran’s nuclear centrifuges got taken out by a computer worm called Stuxnet , thought to have been brought in on a USB stick. AI can also give the military false intelligence , which could lead to irreparable actions.

The good news here is that nuclear stockpiles are down. But they are still enough perhaps to take out half of us . And it wouldn’t be by the nuclear blast itself, but the famine in the nuclear winter that would follow.

Perhaps the most likely risk is that we take ourselves out. And AI might precipitate this.

Imagine – and it doesn’t take a lot of imagination – that AI causes massive job losses , pollutes the information space with misinformation , fractures our politics and destroys human relationships with fake synthetic companionship .

Society might easily break. Slowly but surely, we’d stop being able to support human life at any scale.

What then to take away from all these scenarios? There are some things to be worried about for sure. But not to be too worried, I hope.

Toby Walsh is professor of AI, research group leader at the University of New South Wales. He is the author of God AI: Boom or Doom? What to Expect When Machines Outsmart Us . This article originally appeared in the Conversation

editorials.title: Could we be about to see the end of northern English dialects? My experience – and the science – says aye
editorials.passage:
A t our wedding reception 15 years ago, my new father-in-law stood up, pint in hand, looked me squarely in the eye and welcomed me to the family – and to Yorkshire . He acknowledged my obvious defect – my London roots – before offering a note of comfort. “Don’t worry, Zahaan,” he said. “You’ll fit in here eventually. It’ll just take 50 years.” He added that if I’d been from Lancashire, there’d have been an extra zero on that 50.

Not long after the wedding, my wife and I relocated from our first place together in London to her beautiful home city of York. The quality of life and the glorious scenery on our doorstep have made the move more than worth it – but over the last decade and a half, it’s felt like the people of Yorkshire and I haven’t always spoken the same language.

My untrained southern ear quickly decided they all sounded like a cross between Sean Bean in Game of Thrones and former Spice Girl Mel B. It was, of course, a gross oversimplification – but for someone who had previously treated Watford as the edge of the known universe, it was the best I could do.

It wasn’t just how things sounded that caught me out – some words meant something else entirely up north. In the south, “kegs” are what you store beer in; in parts of Yorkshire, they are your trousers. When I was first offered “tea” up in Yorkshire, I imagined a hot drink, perhaps with a small plate of chocolate biscuits on the side. What actually arrived, of course, was a full evening meal. And that was after I’d had my “dinner” for lunch.

My own children now speak with a proper Yorkshire accent – and mercilessly tease me for my southern tones. I pronounce the green stuff on our lawn “gr-arse”. They say it as if the “a” is barely there. The same goes for “bath”: mine comes out “bar-th”, theirs stays clipped and short. They won’t let it go, repeating my words back to me and comically lengthening my vowels until the whole kitchen is laughing. Whenever I try to defend myself, they look at me as if I’m an amiable foreign exchange student who hasn’t grasped the basics.

That sense of not quite fitting in has never fully worn off. At school pick-ups, if I overhear another parent with a London accent, something switches on in me – a kind of homing beacon – and I find myself gravitating towards them. I feel as if I’ve bumped into a long lost friend. I’ll want to talk about the tube or the price of a two-bedroom flat in Hammersmith or the best curry house – anything London-related. And, perhaps for their benefit or mine, I’ve caught myself deliberately dialling up my own London accent, with more elongated vowels than I might normally use.

Over the years, I’ve never tried to change how I speak, and I certainly haven’t been trying to fake being a northerner. Yet, without me ever quite noticing, some things have changed. I recently offered someone directions to Tadcaster Road and, without thinking, completely forgot to pronounce the “arse” in the middle. And I’ve now started calling dinner “tea” – much to the amusement of my children. This kind of flexing is not uncommon: Andy Burnham, the “king of the north” himself, has been observed sounding more scouse in Liverpool and rather more Mancunian in Manchester.

So where do I belong? When I take the train between York and London, where along the 170-mile journey does “grass” become “gr-arse” and vice versa? On the way up, I still feel like a Londoner heading north. On the way down, oddly, I feel like a northerner heading away from home. In fact, it feels as if I’m not fully northern or southern any more.

Perhaps one of the reasons I struggle to know where I belong is because accents themselves are changing. Dialect boundaries are not fixed lines on a map. They behave much more like bubbles in a bath (pronounced “bath” or “bar-th”; your choice), distinct when left alone but merging and reshaping wherever they touch.

There are in fact some researchers – James Burridge and Tamsin Blaxter among them – who predict that this bubble behaviour may lead to many northern linguistic traits dissolving over time. The word “strut”, for instance, is steadily losing its rhyme with “foot” across parts of the north. And the old northern word for autumn, “backend” – now rarely used – will one day vanish altogether. Not every feature will budge: a 2024 study of the East Midlands, where the north and south bubbles touch, found the boundary between “gr-arse” and “grass” has stayed remarkably stable . While a 2020 study suggested that among city-dwellers in the north, local accents are softening into a more homogenous pan-northern accent. It seems that the same thing that’s happened to my accent and vocabulary is happening across the country. People move, marry, have children and absorb one another’s words and pronunciations.

As it happens, it’s predicted some of these changes could happen within the next 50 years – meaning my father-in-law’s joke may have been more prescient than either of us realised. Plenty of linguistic charm will be lost along the way, no doubt. But perhaps there is a small personal consolation. I may eventually fit in up here – not because I’ll ever talk like Ned Stark, but because there could be far less of a difference between the way people in the north and south speak. Mind you, my children will still find a way to take the mick out of how I say “bar-th”.

Zahaan Bharmal is the author of The Art of Physics and a senior director at Google, writing in a personal capacity

editorials.title: The climate fight has one great ally. You just can’t look at it directly
editorials.passage:
As climate experts from around the world gather in New York for their annual week of talking through the world’s deepest dilemma, the vibes are mostly bad.

Though 2026 seems likely to set a new global temperature record (and 2027, as El Niño gathers steam, is almost certain to break it), and though the planet has careened from one climate disaster to another (European heatwaves that killed tens of thousands, a Nepali flood that wiped out entire communities), and though scientists warn that we’re reaching precisely the global tipping points they’ve long feared (the new research on the faltering great currents of the Atlantic should send a literal chill up your spine), there’s a distinct lack of political momentum.

The host superpower is attacking country after country in search of oily “energy dominance”; even the noblest of its opponents (Canada’s Mark Carney, hope of democratic rebirth in the Americas) is busy building new oil and gas pipelines in the hopes it can bolster his besieged economy. Britain, which finally purged coal power from its energy system last year, now seems poised to start new drilling in the North Sea. If there’s an apocalyptic fear that can still rouse politicians to action, it seems to be AI agents breaking through firewalls, not European nations facing firestorms.

But there is one solitary (and very literal) ray of sunshine amidst this gloom: the steady rise of solar, wind and batteries. That clean energy trinity has broken out of its Chinese base and over the last few years expanded quickly across the planet – from Karachi to California to Cuba, solar panels are going up faster than any energy source has ever grown. It’s even begun to demonstrate that it can drive emissions down: China seems to have started on its downward slope years before most thought it could, and California has cut the use of gas to produce electricity in half in the world’s fourth-largest economy.

None of it is happening fast enough to catch up with the physics of global warming, though – which is precisely why civil society will now try to double down on this one bright spot, and push for a rapid acceleration of clean energy; this transition is going fast, but it needs to go much faster. And it can – China and India are using barely half their solar panel factory capacity, and too many countries are hedging their bets, using clean energy as additional power instead of replacing fossil fuels.

That’s why a group of leading advocates will deliver a letter to the UN this week, urging faster action. The letter offers a clear goal for the entire world to rally around: clean energy access for everyone, everywhere by 2030. And a way to get there: raising funds to bring clean energy to the poorest corners of the world and organizing in our communities, including for a global Sun Day of action next year to kick off what could be the great uniting project of our time.

The signatories range from the most popular active politician in the US (that would be Bernie Sanders) to the most morally grounded spokesperson of the global south (Yeb Saño of the Philippines, say, whose witness after devastating hurricanes helped produce the Paris accords). It comes from great diplomats such as Laurence Tubiana (who helped midwife those Paris agreements) and celebrities and activists such as Jane Fonda. There are leaders from the world of clean energy (Danny Kennedy, for instance, the secretary of the Global Solar Council), and stalwarts from the continents most damaged by rising temperatures (South Africa’s Kumi Naidoo, president of the Fossil Fuel Treaty Initiative). Clean energy entrepreneurs, such as Muhammad Mustafa Amjad of Renewables First in Pakistan, but also the world’s most famous rock climber, Alex Honnold, who runs his own solar non-profit. As they write:

double quotation mark The path forward is difficult, but the way is clear. We want solar for everyone, everywhere, before the decade is out.

We know that standing up to the powerful can be scary. But if there is one thing that unites us, it is that we live beneath the same sun. That unity is our strength, and we must use it to act now.

The letter will be accompanied by the unveiling of a giant mural near the celebrated High Line in New York City. The message is simple, but its three words convey the solution to so many of the interlocking crises we now face: clean energy now.

By the time advocates gather for next year’s New York Climate Week, the landscape may be very different. The physical landscape (there is, I fear, no doubt that El Niño will change the literal map of the world), and the political landscape. If a resurgent movement demands action, we finally have the tools to make that demand matter – a working planet that runs mostly on sun and wind is in tantalizing reach. At the last possible moment, with backs to the wall, we still have our face to the sun.

Bill McKibben is the Schumann distinguished scholar at Middlebury College. He is the founder of Third Act, organizing people over 60 for progressive change

editorials.title: Our message to global leaders: we need solar power everywhere by the decade’s end
editorials.passage:
We the undersigned write this letter out of great fear and great hope.

Over the last few months, we’ve seen the world set ablaze by both war and warming. From the conflict in Iran, which has claimed thousands of lives and disrupted billions more, to the series of ever worsening climate disasters, from wildfires in Europe to collapsing glaciers in Nepal, the world seems to be falling apart exactly when it needs to be coming together.

We know that these crises are connected. The oil that governments fight over is also the carbon pollution that is warming our climate. The bad air quality in Delhi, the high price of fuel in Vietnam, the cost of electricity in the United States, the terrifying floods in the Himalayas – they all connect back to fossil fuels.

Until we end that dependence, we’ll never be able to address the climate emergency and stop fighting these endless oil-soaked wars. That’s why today we are inviting the world to unite around a common cause: repowering the world with cheap, clean energy.

We are calling on governments, businesses, institutions and the public to work together to provide clean, affordable energy to everyone, everywhere by 2030.

From the nearly 1 billion people who still lack access to reliable electricity, to the billions more of us who pay too much for dirty fossil fuels.

We know this world is within reach.

Building clean energy is now the cheapest and fastest way to slash energy bills, reduce pollution, and provide electricity access to the places that need it most.

With cheap solar, wind and batteries, we can create huge and rapid change.

California is already using just half as much natural gas to generate electricity as it did three years ago, thanks to solar and batteries. In Pakistan, people have put up millions of solar panels in just months, relying on social media for instruction. Each month, millions more people across sub-Saharan Africa are getting electricity for the first time with home solar kits.

This energy transition is already moving quickly – but we need it to go much quicker. And so we come together to urge two steps.

First, we must build clean power for everyone. For the first time ever, we can reliably bring electricity to the one in 10 people on earth living without regular access.

We ask everyone who can afford it to donate something so that others can turn the lights on for studying, cooking and medical care – and never have to think about a gallon of diesel or gas again. It takes just $15 to give access to clean electricity for one person for a generation.

Second, we need to build clean power everywhere, and to make that happen, we need to build a movement powerful and beautiful enough to force governments to take large-scale action.

Individual steps alone are not enough: too many of our leaders will resist action until we demonstrate together how much we want them to move. We must demand that governments stop building coal, oil and gas projects we no longer need, and start building the clean-energy systems that works – no pollution or wars required.

One important day along this path will be 20 June, as the summer solstice approaches in the northern hemisphere, generating the most solar power of any day on earth yet. We will celebrate that day as Sun Day, coming together to celebrate and accelerate this great shift.

The path forward is difficult, but the way is clear. We want solar for everyone, everywhere, before the decade is out.

We know that standing up to the powerful can be scary. But if there is one thing that unites us, it is that we live beneath the same sun. That unity is our strength, and we must use it to act now.
